" alt= " This Canadian-designed power storage and conversion device is made to connect to multiple sources of energy to charge a large bank of internal batteries for backup power . " data-portal-copyright= " Steve Maxwell " **28;7143;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1034753 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Slowly but surely , the Canadian electrical system is changing . On the generation side of the equation there&amp;rsquo ; s more solar and wind power coming on stream across the country . But small equipment that boosts electricity independence for end users is changing , too . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I&amp;rsquo ; m always surprised how many people have a deep interest in making their own electricity at a household level . I&amp;rsquo ; m sure the attraction is about more than just economics , too . While big electricity bills are scary , there&amp;rsquo ; s more than just financial fear at work . Quite apart from saving money , many of us feel an attraction to being somewhat self-reliant with a commodity as basic as electricity . It simply feels good knowing you&amp;rsquo ; re not completely dependent on some faceless company out there at the end of the wires . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One of the main refinements to come along lately in the world of home-grown electricity is what I call storage and conversion technologies . If you produce your own power with a windmill or solar panels , then you need to be able to store that electricity for use later . And stored electricity isn&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily something that can power the lights , small appliances , computers and fridges in your life . That&amp;rsquo ; s where conversion comes in. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The best storage-and-conversion equipment I&amp;rsquo ; ve seen so far uses several 12 volt batteries of the size you might find in a car . As with all batteries , the stored power is in the form of direct current ( DC ) . Trouble is , most of our electrical world is made to run on alternating current ( AC ) . You can have a ton of energy stored in batteries , but it won&amp;rsquo ; t be able to operate your microwave , water pump , light bulbs or computer . To make that happen , the DC needs to be converted to the right voltage and frequency of AC . Generically speaking , this job is done by something called an inverter . Sounds complicated ? It isn&amp;rsquo ; t because this technology is getting simpler for end users . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Xantrex ( &lt;a href= " http : //www.xantrex.co " &gt;www.xantrex.c ... m ) is a BC-based company that&amp;rsquo ; s at the leading edge of the kind of equipment that lets people become more energy independent . For the last few months I&amp;rsquo ; ve been working with their PowerHub 1800 battery powered inverter and it&amp;rsquo ; s the best I&amp;rsquo ; ve seen so far . While it&amp;rsquo ; s specially made to connect to solar and wind installations , it serves a useful purpose for anyone connected only to the grid , too . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;7173;TOOLONG ... title= " The first of its kind in the world , this backup electricity source is designed in British Columbia and uses as many as four large batteries to provide hours of operation for household electrical devices " alt= " The first of its kind in the world , this backup electricity source is designed in British Columbia and uses as many as four large batteries to provide hours of operation for household electrical devices " data-portal-copyright= " Steve Maxwell " **28;7209;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1034754 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Imagine a very high capacity uninterruptible power supply ( UPS ) of the sort you might use to protect your computer . Equipment like this keeps sensitive gear safe from electrical surges , and keeps it running when electricity flickers ON and OFF . As soon as the power goes out , even for a few milliseconds , AC power converted from the battery is delivered as needed . In one way , the PowerHub is like a UPS , but much longer lasting , more powerful and more versatile . Instead of just keeping your computer running with a few hundred watts of power for a few minutes , as a standard UPS does , the PowerHub could keep your laptop operating for more than 100 hours . It&amp;rsquo ; ll keep an 18 cubic foot freezer going for 30 hours and it&amp;rsquo ; ll power a sump pump for more than 8 hours of continuous operation . Maximum continuous power output on this device is 1440 watts &amp;ndash ; similar to an ordinary 120-volt wall outlet . It&amp;rsquo ; s like your own private , household battery pack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This unit is quite rightly called a &amp;ldquo ; hub&amp;rdquo ; because it&amp;rsquo ; s made to accept incoming power from different sources . It&amp;rsquo ; s also the first device in the world that accepts power generated on site with wind , solar or a backup generator , as well as power from the grid . It was also exclusively designed in Canada , too . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our world faces energy challenges , but the solutions are on the rise at the same time . Look around and you&amp;rsquo ; ll find more than a few new things that&amp;rsquo ; ll let you have fun boosting your energy independence . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;Steve Maxwell helps people manage their energy lives , houses , gardens and homes at BaileyLineRoad.com . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;8135;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 827810 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa Fire Services Chief Peter McBride was in Mirabel , Que. , on Wednesday to lead a $4-million effort to apply the latest science and technology to firefighting. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An international team of researchers set three structures on fire , and firefighters from Ottawa , Montreal and Mirabel used techniques , informed by a modern understanding of fire dynamics , to douse them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some of the techniques are counterintuitive. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In one case , a fire was set in the living room of a small , empty bungalow . With the front windows of the bungalow wide open , and the living room engulfed , firefighters deployed a powerful fan to the back door of the bungalow and directed a massive flow of air into the building . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Why would firefighters intentionally add oxygen to a fire ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Peter McBride , Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s division chief of safety and innovation , said the technique , known as a positive pressure attack , forces smoke and heat out the open windows , and provides firefighters with a safe corridor to attack the fire with water . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It means firefighters are not standing in smoke that can light up around them . They won&amp;rsquo ; t be in the heat , &amp;rdquo ; explained McBride , who served as project manager for this week&amp;rsquo ; s series of fire experiments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The three test fires conducted Wednesday were recorded on cameras and measured by heat sensors . The responses of firefighters were videotaped for instructional purposes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; All of the material will form part of a new firefighting curriculum being developed by the National Fire Protection Association . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The curriculum , which is to be introduced across Canada next year , is designed to provide firefighters with an up-to-date understanding of fire dynamics , and to equip them with strategies for identifying and attacking different kinds of fires . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another of Wednesday&amp;rsquo ; s test burns saw firefighters set a mattress on fire in a second-floor bedroom of a two-storey home . In the past , firefighters would try to put out such a blaze by dragging hoses into the house to pour water directly on the fire . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;8165;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa Fire Services lead an international training exercise in Mirabel , Quebec , as part of a project that is leading the way in safety and innovation for firefighting . " alt= " Ottawa Fire Services lead an international training exercise in Mirabel , Quebec , as part of a project that is leading the way in safety and innovation for firefighting . During the demonstration fire , firefighters directed the stream off the ceiling of the bedroom in a strategy known as a transitional attack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s like a big sprinkler when it hits the ceiling , &amp;rdquo ; explained McBride. &amp;ldquo ; It throws water in all directions , drops the temperature in that compartment and makes it easier for the fire department to get up there , instead of trying to fight our way up there . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the final experiment of the day , firefighters used a new piece of technology , known as a PyroLance , to douse a fire in a hard-to-reach attic . The PryroLance &amp;mdash ; it looks like a giant pressure washer &amp;mdash ; blasts water and crushed granite in a powerful stream that can cut through wood and steel . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the test , the PyroLance was used to quickly bore a hole in the floor of a burning attic . The device then sprayed a fine , high-pressure mist that knocked down the flames . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The experiments , funded largely by the federal government&amp;rsquo ; s Canadian Safety and Security Program , will inform a new curriculum for Canadian firefighters . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; McBride said the new curriculum will give firefighters the tools they need to deal safely with the modern fire environment . NewsSuzuki : Meeting our greenhouse gas targets requires a ' Leap'http : **34;8278;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;8314;TOOLONG ... title= " Alberta Premier Rachel Notley , left , was part of the Canadian delegation at the COP21 climate talks in Paris on Nov. 30 , 2015. " alt= " Alberta Premier Rachel Notley , left , was part of the Canadian delegation at the COP21 climate talks in Paris on Nov. 30 , 2015. " data-portal-copyright= " Patrick Lachance , Government of Quebec . " **28;8350;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 807119 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; I&amp;rsquo ; m a proud signatory and supporter of the &lt;a href= " https : **33;8380;TOOLONG ... Manifesto&lt;/a&gt; , which takes the challenge of climate change and the 2015 Paris Agreement seriously . It&amp;rsquo ; s been shocking to see the response within the NDP and national media . For like Pope Francis&amp;rsquo ; s 2015 encyclical , Laudato si , Leap enfolds social justice , employment , poverty and hunger , inequity and the environment to map a way out of the crisis we face . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alberta Premier Rachel Notley and B.C. Premier Christy Clark accompanied Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the COP 21 meetings in Paris last year as Canadians applauded Canada&amp;rsquo ; s serious approach to climate change . With the rest of the world , we signed a promise to reduce greenhouse gas emissions so global average temperatures don&amp;rsquo ; t rise beyond 2&amp;nbsp ; degrees&amp;nbsp ; Celsius ( preferably closer to 1.5 Celsius ) above pre-industrial temperatures . The planet has already warmed by close to 1&amp;nbsp ; degree&amp;nbsp ; Celsius , mostly because of the huge increase in fossil fuel use over the past few decades , so meeting the Paris target will be an enormous challenge . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I was ecstatic when Notley won the Alberta election . It appeared we finally had an Alberta government that accepts climate change as real , requiring a radical shift to bring the province&amp;rsquo ; s resource exploitation and economy into balance . If all the ecological repercussions of oilsands development remained within Alberta&amp;rsquo ; s borders , I could understand Notley&amp;rsquo ; s resentment of outside input . But the fate of global climate will be influenced by what she does with the oilsands , so Leap deserves serious consideration . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Climatologists say we must quickly reduce greenhouse gas emissions . Meeting the Paris target will affect every part of society because modern society runs on energy . To have a reasonable chance of meeting the &amp;nbsp ; target , we have to leave most known fossil-fuel reserves in the ground . That means there&amp;rsquo ; s no need to search for more . We must also end subsidies to the fossil-fuel industry , already the most profitable sector in history , and begin a massive energy-conservation program . ( After the 2011 Fukushima meltdown , Japanese people voluntarily reduced their energy use by 25 per cent , a decrease that has persisted for five years. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s biggest emissions reductions resulted from Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s phase-out of carbon-intensive coal plants , a plan Alberta Premier Notley is now embracing . We must go much further , and stop drilling for oil and gas in ecologically sensitive areas such as&amp;nbsp ; the deep ocean and Arctic , halt risky methods like fracking , and wean off high-carbon sources such as&amp;nbsp ; coal and oilsands . We need to curtail investments in fossil fuel infrastructure such as pipelines , rail and roads and coal terminals , because once they&amp;rsquo ; re built , they&amp;rsquo ; ll be used for decades . Premier Clark castigates opponents of her pet project of liquefying high-carbon fracked gas as &amp;ldquo ; forces of No. &amp;rdquo ; But we are really the forces of &amp;ldquo ; know . &amp;rdquo ; We know the necessary steps are not radical or revolutionary but are the logical outcome of the Paris Agreement . Leap offers a path to a safer , better society and a way to meet the Paris commitment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fossil fuels are incredibly energy-rich and convenient , ideal for energy-hungry industrialized societies . For generations , an entire infrastructure has been built around this cheap fuel source . But the economic system that has come to dominate the world failed to factor in the ecological costs of our activities . For close to 95 per cent of human existence , a planet rich in biodiversity readily absorbed the gases released by the fires of nomadic hunter-gatherers . Now , more than seven billion people releasing carbon effluents from powerful oil- and coal-burning machinery overwhelm that capacity . This is the Anthropocene : &amp;nbsp ; We are now the major factor altering the physical , chemical and biological properties of the planet on a geological scale . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The impacts of anthropogenic climate change are obvious to all but those blinded by self-interest or fear . It won&amp;rsquo ; t be easy to transition to renewable energy . But all who care about the fate of future generations have the greatest stake in dealing with climate change , and we can no longer dither for political , religious or economic reasons . We&amp;rsquo ; ve already failed to heed the urgent warnings for close to three decades . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meeting the Paris targets will have consequences for fossil-fuel industry workers , which is why the government must step in to protect them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The &lt;a href= " https : **33;8415;TOOLONG ... Manifesto&lt;/a&gt; hints at the massive opportunities that lie in utilizing the skills developed in drilling , pipefitting , electrical work and transportation for jobs in renewable energy . Indeed , once the challenge is grasped , as Canadian Labour Congress president Hassan Yussuff recently announced , we can aim for one&amp;nbsp ; million jobs in five years in renewable energy and clean technology . Oilsands worker Lliam Hildebrand is executive director of Iron and Earth , a group that proposes to train thousands of workers to install solar panels on schools and create other opportunities in renewable energy . I can&amp;rsquo ; t overemphasize the benefits that will arise from making the commitment to meet the Paris Agreement&amp;rsquo ; s obligations . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The whole notion of jobs versus the environment is as outdated as our fossil-fuelled system . If we want to save both the climate and the economy , we have to Leap . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **29;8450;TOOLONG Suzuki&lt;/strong&gt; is an award-winning scientist , environmentalist and broadcaster . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; David SuzukiWed , 04 May 2016 14:40:46 **45;8481;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;8598;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 803933 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Algonquin College asked one of the world&amp;rsquo ; s biggest engineering companies to help it save&amp;nbsp ; energy , no one at the college expected to start&amp;nbsp ; generating two million watts of their own electricity . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The big yellow&amp;nbsp ; cogeneration unit&amp;nbsp ; ( meaning it burns natural gas to generate both electricity and heat for buildings at the same time ) is now a reality . The tour of VIPs in clean and gleaming&amp;nbsp ; hardhats is over . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And the result puts Algonquin a big step ahead of the usual energy-saving plans that concentrate mainly on&amp;nbsp ; better windows , low-energy lightbulbs and low-flow toilets . ( Algonquin , as it happens , is doing those things too. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The cogen unit , as it&amp;rsquo ; s known , &amp;ldquo ; was something the college didn&amp;rsquo ; t even consider&amp;rdquo ; when it asked companies&amp;nbsp ; for proposals , said&amp;nbsp ; Todd Schonewille , the college&amp;rsquo ; s director of physical resources . &amp;ldquo ; But Siemens put together a pretty compelling vision of how this would fit in with our overall energy modelling for the campus . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That was in 2012 . Construction for the cogen unit began in earnest last summer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The waste heat from the power generator does two things . In winter , it heats buildings . No surprise there . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But in summer , this heat&amp;nbsp ; actually cools them . &amp;nbsp ; The system is&amp;nbsp ; called an absorption chiller , and it uses leftover&amp;nbsp ; heat from the generator to power&amp;nbsp ; a chemical process to&amp;nbsp ; bring down the air temperature . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This means that the generating&amp;nbsp ; system will be running at highest&amp;nbsp ; levels in summer and winter , when it is cost-effective because of the&amp;nbsp ; cooling and heating . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And there&amp;rsquo ; s more on the horizon : Some solar power still to come , and the potential for a second two-megawatt generator . ( A megawatt is one million watts . ) The college&amp;rsquo ; s peak power use comes in September , at about four million watts , and it reaches about three million watts in winter . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The new technology is also&amp;nbsp ; a teaching tool for Algonquin students . &amp;nbsp ; Ontario has just approved the college&amp;rsquo ; s new certificate program in energy management , which is an immediate fit . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The power produced at Algonquin stays at Algonquin , unlike home-variety solar panels that usually send power to Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s grid . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An interpretive centre just outside the plant will show staff and students minute-by-minute figures on power production and usage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The entire project , which encompasses major changes to energy use throughout the campus , &amp;nbsp ; is supposed to pay for itself through&amp;nbsp ; energy savings in&amp;nbsp ; 20 years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **28;8628;TOOLONG " **35;8658;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : //twitter.com/TomSpears1 " &gt;twitt ... &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Tom Spears , Ottawa CitizenWed , 27 Apr 2016 19:43:18 **45;8695;TOOLONG ... The core concept of converting sunlight into electricity remains the same . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We came up with a tracking system that uses very , very inexpensive components , &amp;rdquo ; said Dupuis. &amp;ldquo ; These are components you can buy off the shelf at any electronics store . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This technology that we developed is not new or groundbreaking in the sense that we invented new tech . BusinessLocal NewsCoon Come : Do n't leave Indigenous Peoples out of climate change planhttp : **36;8964;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;9002;TOOLONG ... title= " Matthew Coon Come , Grand Chief , Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee ( Quebec ) , writes that climate change is a human rights issues for Indigenous Peoples . " alt= " Matthew Coon Come , Grand Chief , Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee ( Quebec ) , writes that climate change is a human rights issues for Indigenous Peoples . " data-portal-copyright= " John Kenney " **28;9038;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 771332 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; I had the privilege last&amp;nbsp ; week of attending the First Ministers Conference on Climate Change with the prime minister , provincial premiers and Indigenous leaders . We heard very positive statements about the need for a low-carbon economy , the importance of Indigenous peoples&amp;rsquo ; connection to our traditional lands , the importance of establishing nation-to-nation relations , and generally following through on commitments to raise the priority of addressing fundamental Indigenous issues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There was an implicit recognition , I believe , that climate change has an impact on Indigenous Peoples&amp;rsquo ; human rights . As Indigenous peoples , we have a very small ecological footprint in terms of climate change&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; yet it has been repeatedly confirmed globally that we are among the most vulnerable to its negative effects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the recent climate change talks in Paris , the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights ( OHCHR ) emphasized : &amp;ldquo ; &amp;hellip ; negative impacts will increase exponentially according to the degree of climate change that ultimately takes place and will disproportionately affect individuals , groups and peoples in vulnerable situations including &amp;hellip ; indigenous peoples . &amp;rdquo ; The OHCHR added : &amp;ldquo ; Simply put , climate change is a human rights problem and the human rights framework must be part of the solution . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is beyond dispute that climate change&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; arising from human activities&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; is causing profound impacts on a wide range of human rights . These include the rights to life , self-determination , development , security , culture , food , health , water and sanitation and housing . We live on the land . Land is our identity . We will feel the effects of climate change in every aspect of our lives . &amp;nbsp ; By impacting our lands , territories and resources , our Treaty rights and our cultures as distinct Indigenous Peoples will be seriously affected . &amp;nbsp ; In some cases , such harmful actions are likely to be irreversible . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Therefore , it is imperative that climate change strategies and actions taken by First Ministers in Canada fundamentally include a human rights-based approach that fully respects Indigenous Peoples . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Understanding Human Rights and Climate Change , the OHCHR indicated : &amp;ldquo ; Particular care should be taken to comply with relevant human rights obligations related to participation of persons , groups and peoples in vulnerable situations in decision-making processes and to ensure that adaptation and mitigation efforts do not have adverse effects on those that they should be protecting . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Further , to the extent that any Canadian initiatives are developed to address climate change that derive from the way in which natural resources are extracted , particularly where those natural resources are located on traditional Indigenous lands , we need to be involved . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If there is economic and financial gain related to the way in which natural resources situated on traditional Indigenous lands are exploited , or not exploited , Indigenous Peoples need to have a voice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For example , forest stands absorb carbon dioxide and contribute to reductions in greenhouse gases and their protection is , therefore , important in the fight against climate change . Any organization , institution or company that sets aside forest lands for protection increases the availability of carbon credits to trade on the international carbon trading market , thus benefitting financially from conservation initiatives . &amp;nbsp ; Indigenous Peoples need to be involved in the valuable non-exploitation of natural resources in the same way that we need to be involved if those natural resources were being extracted . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; We , of course , applaud any initiatives that result in a reduction of harmful emissions of pollutants into the environment . We applaud initiatives that&amp;nbsp ; contribute to the fight against climate change . And , we applaud initiatives that&amp;nbsp ; result in conservation measures related to the natural resources on our traditional lands . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; However , to the extent that financial gain is made in the way in which natural resources within our traditional lands are dealt with , in any manner , our peoples need to be part of that discussion , part of those formulae and we need to be at those tables together with the provinces and the companies that stand to gain from cap-and-trade and other carbon reduction schemes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **31;9068;TOOLONG Coon Come&lt;/strong&gt; is Grand Chief , Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee ( Quebec ) , and former national chief , Assembly of First Nations . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Matthew Coon ComeSun , 06 Mar 2016 14:00:14 **45;9101;TOOLONG ... Here 's how we can help business reduce greenhouse gas emissionshttp : **31;9296;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;9329;TOOLONG ... title= " Jayson Myers , president and CEO of Canadian Manufacturers &amp; Exporters , wants clear incentives to help business battle greenhouse gas emissions . " alt= " Jayson Myers , president and CEO of Canadian Manufacturers &amp; Exporters , wants clear incentives to help business battle greenhouse gas emissions . " data-portal-copyright= " Ashley Fraser " **28;9365;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 769870 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Climate Change is an investment issue . So too is economic growth . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As&amp;nbsp ; Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and the premiers meet in Vancouver in an attempt to coordinate efforts to reduce Canada&amp;rsquo ; s greenhouse gas ( GHG ) emissions , there will be a lot of discussion about the targets that governments should set and the policy instruments best suited to achieving them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They will no doubt consider ways to structure regulations and economic instruments such as&amp;nbsp ; carbon taxes and cap-and-trade systems . &amp;nbsp ; Several first ministers will come to the table with their own preferred approaches . But , all need to be concerned about the consequences of their decisions . Collectively , their challenge will be to come up with a plan that achieves desired emission reductions while at the same time sustaining economic growth . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the course of their deliberations , our leaders would do well to look at the evidence of the past 25 years . Since 1990 , the Canadian economy has expanded at an average rate of 2.5 per cent per year . GHG emissions across Canada have increased at an average annual rate of 0.6 percent over that same period of time . The difference , which is the rate of reduction in emission intensity ( emissions generated per unit of economic activity ) , reflects technological progress : improvements in energy efficiency , the substitution of less carbon-intensive fuels , the adoption of less carbon-intensive industrial processes and land use management practices , and the construction of more carbon-efficient energy and transportation infrastructure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There has been no direct relationship between higher carbon prices and reductions in emission intensity over the past 25 years . Our emissions from transportation , for instance , continued to grow even as gasoline prices reached record highs . It is also apparent that a downturn in economic activity does not necessarily lead to lower emission levels . &amp;nbsp ; Output in Canada&amp;rsquo ; s manufacturing sector fell by 25 per cent during the 2008-09 recession , but contrary to widespread opinion , manufacturing emissions actually rose . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , the opposite is true . &amp;nbsp ; The most rapid rates of emission intensity reduction have been achieved during periods of strong economic growth . &amp;nbsp ; The key factor has been capital investment in new and improved housing and building construction , machinery and equipment , and public infrastructure . The lesson is that higher rates of investment accelerate emission intensity reductions . &amp;nbsp ; And , when investment declines , emissions increase . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our leaders should take this experience to heart . If Canadians are to meet our current target of reducing GHG emissions 30 per cent below present levels by 2030 , we need to triple the rate of technological progress . In turn , that will require a higher rate of capital investment and more targeted investments in more productive and carbon-efficient technologies . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Whether regulation , carbon tax , or cap and trade , none of these options will be effective in achieving emission reduction targets ( whatever they may be ) if they are not accompanied by measures that encourage capital investment . In fact , they are apt to do a lot of economic and environmental damage on their own if they divert money that could otherwise be invested by consumers or industry in new technologies into general government revenues or high-risk technology unicorns with little chance of commercial success or widespread adoption here in Canada . It&amp;rsquo ; s important to keep in mind that for every dollar profits are reduced , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s business sector invests approximately $1.40 less in buildings , technology and equipment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What is required instead is a concerted , cross-government policy approach that : &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ndash ; Provides tax and financial incentives to consumers and businesses that invest in and adopt more productive , less emission intensive products and technologies ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ndash ; Funds the construction of smarter , more efficient energy and transportation infrastructure ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ndash ; Reduces regulatory impediments to putting new technologies and infrastructure in place ; and , &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ndash ; Ensures that industrial investment in Canada is not lost to other jurisdictions only to generate even more emissions elsewhere . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; These are the types of policy measures that would be good for the economy as well as for the environment . &amp;nbsp ; They would boost productivity , help stimulate economic growth , and accelerate the adoption of less carbon-intensive technologies which is essential in achieving actual emission reductions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Let&amp;rsquo ; s not confuse the introduction of regulations , carbon taxes , or cap and trade for real progress in reducing GHG emissions . They may be part of the solution , but only if accompanied by measures that encourage investment and accelerate technological progress . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **30;9395;TOOLONG Myers&lt;/strong&gt; is president and CEO , Canadian Manufacturers &amp; Exporters&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Jayson MyersWed , 02 Mar 2016 17:51:52 **45;9427;TOOLONG ... Fossil fuel subsidies weaken the climate change plan , prime ministerhttp : **32;9474;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;9508;TOOLONG ... title= " In Paris , Canadian Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna Minister Catherine McKenna signed -- along with 39 other countries including the United States -- a fossil fuel subsidy reform communiqu ? . " alt= " In Paris , Canadian Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna Minister Catherine McKenna signed -- along with 39 other countries including the United States -- a fossil fuel subsidy reform communiqu ? . " data-portal-copyright= " Adrian Wyld " **28;9544;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 769826 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s leadership at the December Paris climate change conference was dramatic and impressive . Prime Minister Justin Trudeau , &amp;nbsp ; together with five premiers and many provincial and territorial ministers , &amp;nbsp ; sent a strong , unambiguous signal that tackling climate change is urgent . Three months after Paris , the hard work of translating ambition to action continues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The&amp;nbsp ; prime minister is now at the second of two First Ministers&amp;rsquo ; meetings to lay out steps towards a Pan-Canadian climate plan . A few days from now , U.S. President Barack Obama will host the prime minister in Washington , where joint action to tackle climate change will loom large . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The centrepiece of a national climate plan will be a carbon price . Intense debate continues around the level of ambition of a tax , as well as where revenues should flow . However , before any carbon price is introduced , Ottawa needs to ensure that those efforts are not weakened by its own continued support for fossil fuel subsidies . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our federal and provincial governments provide roughly&amp;nbsp ; $2.9 billion in subsidies to the fossil fuel sector . These are mainly through tax breaks , for example to encourage oil and gas exploration , or to accelerate how capital cost allowances are calculated . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the global level , roughly $500 billion U.S. is spent each year to support fossil fuel consumption . In many countries , more is spent to subsidize fossil fuels than on hospitals and schooling . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Given the short timeframe for a carbon price , it&amp;rsquo ; s urgent that fossil fuel subsidies are identified and removed quickly . &amp;nbsp ; Sixteen&amp;nbsp ; years ago , Finance Canada promised to&amp;nbsp ; be explicit in how it&amp;nbsp ; calculated fossil fuel subsidies . We are still awaiting that report . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Maintaining fossil fuel subsidies will weaken or offset the intended pricing effect that a carbon price will exert . Looking at the other side , eliminating fossil fuel subsidies will help level the playing field for clean , low-carbon renewable energy . It would open up fiscal space for new investments in a new generation of green technologies . And it would reduce greenhouse gas emissions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The International Institute for Sustainable Development estimates that a complete phaseout of subsidies for the consumption of fossil fuels would reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by as much as six&amp;nbsp ; to 13 per cent by 2050 . Removing subsidies that support the production of fossil fuels would further increase the impact . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the Paris conference , Minister Catherine McKenna signed&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; along with 39 other countries including the United States&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; a fossil fuel subsidy reform communiqu&amp;eacute ; . In that communiqu&amp;eacute ; , Canada endorsed three principles : be transparent about where fossil fuel subsidies exist ; be ambitious in their reform ; and provide targeted support to those that are vulnerable to higher energy prices . The task now is to act . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; With respect to transparency , the government should communicate a clear picture of the scale of Canadian producer and consumer subsidies for fossil fuels , following internationally recognized criteria . A&amp;nbsp ; process should then be launched that brings together stakeholders for a bottom-up policy discussion on how reform should proceed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On ambition , the government should outline a timeframe for how it will proceed with phasing out fossil fuel subsidies , and a set a date for when the process will be complete . Canada , along with the other G20 countries , has already committed to phasing out &amp;ldquo ; inefficient&amp;rdquo ; fossil fuel subsidies , and there is growing pressure to attach a date to that pledge . By committing to an end-date at home , Canada would provide&amp;nbsp ; impetus to other G20 countries to do the same . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finally , special effort must be made to ensure that communities that are vulnerable to fossil fuel subsidy reform , such as remote and northern communities , are protected . The government should also engage with the private sector to ensure the transition takes&amp;nbsp ; place in a measured fashion to&amp;nbsp ; mitigate potential economic risks and threats to competitiveness . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is a unique moment in Canadian history , as governments , businesses and communities look to a new generation of low-carbon energy solutions . The current structure of incentives that include fossil fuel subsidies locks in inertia and stifles innovation . Removing these subsidies should be a critical part of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s climate change strategy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **29;9574;TOOLONG Vaughan&lt;/strong&gt; is president of the International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ) , and Canada 's former commissioner of the environment and sustainable development . &lt;strong&gt;Philip Gass&lt;/strong&gt; is a senior researcher with IISD 's Energy Program . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Scott Vaughan , Philip GassWed , 02 Mar 2016 17:36:46 **45;9605;TOOLONG ... councillors want transmission lines ; renewable energy not enough , they sayhttp : **37;9652;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;9691;TOOLONG ... title= " Barrhaven city councillor Jan Harder in 2014. " data-portal-copyright= " STR " **28;11203;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 602207 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Black Monday , everyone seems to be calling it . &amp;nbsp ; Some economists are calling it a slow-motion global meltdown of 2008 proportions . Others are saying this week&amp;rsquo ; s heart-stopping event in Chinese equity markets is merely an overdue and sudden deflation of bloated stock values . But Black Monday it is , in both camps , and in Canada the respectable question the event raises appears to be this one : which of the three main federal election contenders is best suited to steer Canada though a volatile and newly strange global economy ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another question that should not go unconsidered is worth asking precisely because neither Stephen Harper nor Thomas Mulcair nor Justin Trudeau , for their differing reasons , would want it asked too persistently . As impolite as it may be to put the question in these terms , it is about who should be most trusted to keep Canada from the harm that the gluttonous Leninist kleptocracy in Beijing unavoidably causes us all . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Stephen Harper&amp;rsquo ; s Conservatives can not be faulted for failing to possess the gift of clairvoyance , but there has been a cost to Harper&amp;rsquo ; s 2006 declaration that Canada&amp;rsquo ; s destiny was to be an &amp;ldquo ; energy superpower&amp;rdquo ; and to his own stubborn imagining of China as the gold hoard at the end of an oilsands-rich rainbow . Canada has been left both vulnerable to unseemly diplomatic compromises with dirty Chinese money and economically exposed to plummeting resource commodity prices &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; oil , natural gas , copper , coal , iron , the lot . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; During the summer of 2014 , &amp;nbsp ; the North American benchmark price for oil was $105 a barrel . It&amp;rsquo ; s now down to $39 , and the Chinese economy &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; the real one , not the poker championships of equity trading &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; still isn&amp;rsquo ; t all that desperate for our oil , even at these prices . So far this year , China has imported a whopping 6.7 million barrels of crude a day , a jump of 640,000 barrels over last year , but China&amp;rsquo ; s state-owned oil complex is now exporting roughly&amp;nbsp ; 670,000 barrels a day in refined products . The&amp;nbsp ; Chinese economy benefitted from $120 billion in foreign direct investment last year , but another $102.9 billion in Chinese capital flowed out of the country . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s taken too long for the penny to drop , and when the necessity of a policy shift becomes too painfully obvious , Harper has tended to opt for the feint or the sop. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By 2012 , Beijing&amp;rsquo ; s intrusions into outright oilpatch-property ownership had reached such scandalous proportions that Harper was forced , by his own caucus as much as by public opinion , to do something . It took the $15.1 billion takeover of Calgary&amp;rsquo ; s oil-and-gas poster boy Nexen by Chinese state conglomerate CNOOC &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; China&amp;rsquo ; s largest-ever overseas acquisition &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; for Harper to make a move . And even then , he vowed only that the deal would mark the end of a trend . Further takeovers would be discouraged , but according to rules of sufficient opacity to allow the broadest exceptions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It took no small amount of boat-rocking within Harper&amp;rsquo ; s caucus for former Citizenship and Immigration Minister Jason Kenney to get a green light in 2012 to rein in Canada&amp;rsquo ; s most embarrassing ingratiation of Chinese capital &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; the out-of-control Immigrant Investor Program . Taken together with its Quebec version , the IIP scam allowed roughly 50,000 mostly Chinese millionaires to acquire Canadian citizenship over the program&amp;rsquo ; s final decade or so , and to settle down &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; or not &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; in the Canadian real estate they&amp;rsquo ; d acquired , mostly in Metro Vancouver . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two weeks ago , the sop : Harper promised new measures to help&amp;nbsp ; track the property-bubble impacts of &amp;ldquo ; foreign , non-resident&amp;rdquo ; real estate acquisitions in Canada . This is not a bad idea , but it neatly misses the point . The world-class unaffordability of housing in Vancouver shouldn&amp;rsquo ; t be expected to result from the appetites of &amp;ldquo ; foreign&amp;rdquo ; buyers , which count for near to nothing against the impact of all those millionaires who bought their Canadian citizenship papers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nobody quite knows where they all went , anyway . &amp;nbsp ; There are more than 300,000 Canadian citizens living and working in Hong Kong and Mainland China now , and as Ian Young of the South China Morning Post reports , here&amp;rsquo ; s how weird things have gotten in Vancouver , where the average price for a detached house is now $1.4 million : &amp;nbsp ; there are 24,960 households within the city limits with a declared income that is a lesser amount than the cost of the household itself in utilities , property tax , and mortgage or rent . &amp;ldquo ; Think about that , &amp;rdquo ; Young writes , &amp;ldquo ; these households claim to earn less than they spend on accommodation alone . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But if all this makes Harper look a bit lame , Justin Trudeau&amp;rsquo ; s best known pronouncement on China is probably this November 2013 flippancy : &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsqu ... a level of admiration I actually have for China because their basic dictatorship is allowing them to actually turn their economy around on a dime. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Aside from all that , this week&amp;rsquo ; s hemorrhaging of $8 trillion in worldwide wealth &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; $5 trillion just from the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; proves painfully that Beijing&amp;rsquo ; s tyrants can&amp;rsquo ; t quite turn the Chinese economy around on a dime after all . Then there was Trudeau&amp;rsquo ; s weirdness in the lead-up to CNOOC&amp;rsquo ; s takeover of Nexen , when he explained that he was content with the acquisition because his &amp;ldquo ; instincts&amp;rdquo ; told him it was fine , adding &amp;ldquo ; obviously my family has historical ties with China . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As a corrective , last December Trudeau appointed the Beijing-based consultant and former Foreign Affairs bureaucrat&amp;nbsp ; Margaret Cornish as his senior adviser on China . A slight problem , more optics than anything else : in August 2013 the Ontario Superior Court approved an $8.1 million class-action settlement against Cornish and four of her fellow directors of the Zungui Haixi Corporation , a Chinese sportswear and shoe factory . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The class-action settlement was a compromise , and not a finding of wrongdoing by its directors . Cornish and her colleagues denied the allegations against them , and bad things do happen to good people , so let&amp;rsquo ; s be fair . But it isn&amp;rsquo ; t so easy to dismiss the strange enchantment that seems to possess Cornish when it comes to Beijing&amp;rsquo ; s state-owned enterprises . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In&amp;nbsp ; 2012 , Cornish undertook a study for the Canadian Council of Chief Executives that reached conclusions that can best be described as eccentric : Chinese SOEs don&amp;rsquo ; t act like implements of the Chinese Communist Party , they&amp;rsquo ; re &amp;ldquo ; profit driven to their core&amp;rdquo ; and Ottawa should treat them just like any other company . &amp;nbsp ; This flies in the face of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission , the Economist magazine , and even the 5th plenary session of the 15th gathering of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party , which counted on SOE&amp;rsquo ; s to be Beijing&amp;rsquo ; s primary instruments in the party&amp;rsquo ; s overseas-acquisitions strategy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over the past two years , Chinese president Xi Jinping has been tightening his grip on SOEs and running an old-fashioned purge through the companies&amp;rsquo ; ranks . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As for Thomas Mulcair&amp;rsquo ; s New Democrats , there&amp;rsquo ; s not much to be said because they just don&amp;rsquo ; t like talking about China , lest a party candidate says something that someone might construe as &amp;ldquo ; sinophobic. &amp;rdquo ; Mulcair is happy to berate the Conservatives for ratifying the Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement ( and the Liberals for voting with the Conservatives on it ) but he&amp;rsquo ; s less than clear about what a Mulcair government might actually do about it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; During the Chinese government&amp;rsquo ; s buying spree in the Alberta oilpatch the New Democrats were strangely quiet . The NDP has no Bernie Sanders , the left-wing outlier for the Democratic ticket who has raged consistently and understandably that American workers are forced to compete with the captive labour of one-fifth of humanity now controlled by President Xi . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Say what you like about Harper and China . The Opposition leaders have been mostly useless . So if the challenge of coping with China after the polls close October 19 is something that matters to you , you&amp;rsquo ; re on your own . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Terry Glavin is an author and journalist . &lt;/p&gt; Terry GlavinWed , 26 Aug 2015 21:24:36 **45;11233;TOOLONG ... Solar is the new oil . Again . Skies clear this time ? http : **35;12176;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;12213;TOOLONG ... title= " Dick Bakker , president of the Ottawa Renewable Energy Co-operative , stands among the solar panels on the roof of Franco-Cite School on Smyth Road . " alt= " Dick Bakker , president of the Ottawa Renewable Energy Co-operative , stands among the solar panels on the roof of Franco-Cite School on Smyth Road . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;12249;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 546813 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Solar power is threatening to save the world again . And this time , &amp;nbsp ; it&amp;nbsp ; really , really means it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Forget the energy evangelists for a moment &amp;mdash ; trust your own eyes . You can&amp;rsquo ; t swing a cat&amp;nbsp ; in this town without hitting a solar panel . Hydro Ottawa reports that , in just over five years , some 720 renewable energy projects are now feeding the grid , the vast majority being solar . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Take just one school board . The Ottawa public has solar projects at 41 schools and there are plans to add 24 more . The other three boards have a combined 20 projects and growing . The French public board &amp;mdash ; how did this slip by ? &amp;nbsp ; &amp;mdash ; is producing some 1.2 megawatts of electricity , enough to power roughly 200 homes . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;span style= " line-height:1.5 ; " &gt;Loblaw 's , for Pete 's sake , has 62 solar installations in Ontario . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And Bloomberg just reported this astounding fact : in 2013 , for the first time , the world added more renewable energy capacity ( 143 gigawatts ) than oil , coal and natural gas combined ( 141 ) , described as a historic &amp;ldquo ; turning point . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So here we are , on a gorgeous June evening , on the roof of Franco-Cit&amp;eacute ; , a French Catholic high school on Smyth Road , with the&amp;nbsp ; tall , debonair&amp;nbsp ; &lt;span style= " line-height:1.5 ; " &gt;Paolo Maccario , an &lt;/span&gt; &lt;span style= " line-height:1.5 ; " &gt;Italian-born engineer . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He is the general manager of Silfab Ontario Inc. , which manufactured the hundreds of&amp;nbsp ; panels that lie tilted , checkerboard like , on the flat roof . The Mississauga plant now runs 24/7 , he said , and has expanded four times since 2011. &amp;ldquo ; We make four of these in one day , &amp;rdquo ; he said , scanning the 150-kilowatt array , which went online in February . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The story of solar cells , he explained , is comparable to the evolution of the microchip . With enough scale , with continued innovation , they get cheaper and better at an exponentially rapid rate . Not to mention the China effect . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In four years , the price of a solar cell&amp;nbsp ; has dropped&amp;nbsp ; from about $2.20 per watt to 75 cents , he said , a decrease of 66 per cent . And the trend will continue , as solar production is marching&amp;nbsp ; ahead in every corner of the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Maccario was touring the site with Dick Bakker , once an&amp;nbsp ; all-star football lineman with Queen&amp;rsquo ; s University and now the president of Ottawa Renewable Energy Co-Operative , and its treasurer , Johan Hamels , a longtime Green Party activist in Belgium and Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Bakker installed a $70,000 solar grid on his rural property at Manotick Station in 2010 . Today , it would cost less than half and produce&amp;nbsp ; better . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They think the comparison to computers and online networks is apt. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When I was in high school , we worked on a dumb terminal connected to a couple of centralized computers , &amp;rdquo ; said Bakker , in his late 50s. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Now , over the last 40 years , the grid has evolved so that everybody is carrying a main frame in their pocket . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The c0-op , which began in 2010 , now has 400 members who invest sums in exchange for a set return over long periods , usually 20 years . It has nine projects up and running , fully owned or shared , and four more in the pipeline . They are typically in the 150-to-200-kW range &amp;mdash ; much bigger than a household unit , but smaller than industrial monsters . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The co-op stresses the idea of local ownership and fundamentally believes in the wisdom of producing power very close to where it will be consumed . Bakker does not see one &amp;ldquo ; silver bullet&amp;rdquo ; solar solution to Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s energy needs but many varied options of tapping into renewables &amp;mdash ; water , wind and sun . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Much of the progress now depends on the ability of the existing grid to accept the power . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re going to move forward , then sideways a bit , then forward again . It all ties back to the grid and if the grid in that locale is set up ( to accept production ) . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A senior bureaucrat in the Ministry of Energy recently told a conference that&amp;nbsp ; &lt;span style= " line-height:1.5 ; " &gt;Ontario has 1,550 megawatts of solar electricity installed , enough to power roughly 300,000 homes , &lt;/span&gt; &lt;span style= " line-height:1.5 ; " &gt;with another 825 megawatts under way . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There has been controversy , of course , about solar subsidies from taxpayers , which were once at levels some found obscene , especially in an over-supply market . &amp;nbsp ; But , in hand with cheaper setup costs , new contracts for small projects pay 38 cents a kilowatt/hour not 80. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The industry predicts solar will be competitive with other renewables by 2018 . Look at fossil fuel exploration and the trouble with pipelines , they ask : where will the smart money go ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s the money that makes things go around , &amp;rdquo ; says Maccario. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is considerable buzz , as well , about a new generation of sleek-looking batteries built as an offshoot of the Tesla electric car . The batteries , intended for homes , industries and utilities , store power for&amp;nbsp ; the dark hours or when the draw is at peak . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Then again , there is always considerable buzz in solar &amp;mdash ; perfectly sunny somewhere , &amp;nbsp ; even if it&amp;rsquo ; s the future . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; To contact Kelly Egan , please call 613-726-5896 or email &lt;a href= " **30;12279;TOOLONG " **37;12311;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : **29;12350;TOOLONG " &gt; ... &lt;/p&gt; Kelly EganMon , 08 Jun 2015 14:30:10 **45;12381;TOOLONG ... Blind River has tax revenues of $8.8 million per year . The payments to CMHC account for 12 per cent of its annual revenues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Despite promising&amp;nbsp ; to speak to &lt;em&gt;The Citizen&lt;/em&gt; on Wednesday about the lengthy debt burden and the effect it will have on taxpayers in the municipality , Blind River Mayor Sue Jensen failed to return calls to talk about the situation . Elected as mayor in November , Jensen was a town councillor at the time the municipality sought the loan from CMHC and invested part of that money , $25 million , in Plasco. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ottawa-based waste-to-energy firm , which&amp;nbsp ; currently has&amp;nbsp ; court protection from its creditors , has listed North Shore Power Group &amp;mdash ; a Blind River utility &amp;mdash ; as a $17.92-million liability . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I am responsible to the taxpayers &amp;ndash ; and they are very important to me I might add &amp;ndash ; I have been avoiding you as I work full time and talking to the media is not necessarily a regular occurrence for me , &amp;rdquo ; Jensen wrote in an email Tuesday . &amp;ldquo ; I will definitely call you tomorrow &amp;ndash ; March 11 at 1:00 p.m. &amp;ndash ; promise . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The mayor did not keep that promise . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;12684;TOOLONG ... title= " Blind River Mayor Sue Jensen " alt= " Blind River Mayor Sue Jensen " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;12720;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 482038 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Graeme Lowry , president&amp;nbsp ; of North Shore Power Group , stated that he is simply an &amp;ldquo ; employee&amp;rdquo ; of the municipality before declining&amp;nbsp ; to conduct a phone interview . Lowry then requested questions be submitted by email . The questions were answered in the form of a statement by unnamed city staff . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to to the statement , the municipality is confident that North Shore will be able to provide the $1.1-million payments to CMHC on an annual basis as a result of solar electricity it is generating and selling back into Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s power grid . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; ( North Shore ) can pay the new mortgage amortization schedule to the town which will pay it to CMHC , &amp;rdquo ; reads the statement . &amp;ldquo ; We have 121 operating power projects , all over the province of Ontario and we have 5 ( megawatts ) of new projects under construction and development right now . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; With regards to the $22.5 million remaining in debt owed in 2037 , an amount which has been deferred by CMHC at 0 per cent interest until it&amp;rsquo ; s due , the town is confident that any money it recoups from Plasco will help to lower the overall bill . Should no money be recouped from Plasco , then the loan would need to be renegotiated further . The town says it could , in that situation , &amp;nbsp ; ask CMHC to write the loan off once&amp;nbsp ; it comes due . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Should no recovery be earned by ( North Shore ) from Plasco , and this amount remains at its original value , then it is our view that it may be reasonable to expect CMHC may choose to provision for a loan write-down over time , &amp;rdquo ; reads the town&amp;rsquo ; s statement . &amp;ldquo ; As a national lender , this is normal course banking and all loans include risk pricing . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The town&amp;rsquo ; s response comes amid questions over how it&amp;nbsp ; even qualified for a&amp;nbsp ; $49.5-million loan given its relatively small&amp;nbsp ; annual revenues , as well as&amp;nbsp ; why any of the money it received was invested in a start-up company in Ottawa . &amp;nbsp ; To qualify for funding , projects needed to have started after January 2009 . Plasco&amp;rsquo ; s Trail Road plant was built in 2006. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; North Shore claimed the investment made into Plasco was only made after extensive due diligence was conducted by a high-profile Ottawa law firm into the company . However , the law firm distanced itself from the situation , saying it had nothing to do with the town or its investment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; City staff wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t provide detailed information as to what kind of guidance Blind River received before investing in&amp;nbsp ; Plasco . The city staff did say &amp;ldquo ; significant research was conducted by us and by several sophisticated private equity funds . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Blind River initially wanted to build a biomass energy generation plant , using technology similar to that being developed by Plasco . According to an August 2009 article in Northern Ontario Business , a trade publication , the town had spent three years planning as many as three biomass energy projects . However , the rising price of wood needed to fuel the project and the Liberal government&amp;rsquo ; s sudden announcement of the Feed-in Tariff Program , which offered lucrative rates for electricity generated through&amp;nbsp ; solar and other renewable energy sources , prodded Blind River to change its plans . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If someone had told me prior to Christmas that by February I&amp;rsquo ; d have the whole thing rewritten into a solar plant , I&amp;rsquo ; d have told them they were absolutely out of their mind . It couldn&amp;rsquo ; t be done , &amp;rdquo ; Stoney Burton , general manager of Blind River Development Corp. , told the publication at the time . &amp;ldquo ; But , we did it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was the solar plan that was submitted to CMHC a few months later and ultimately approved by the federal housing regulator for funding under the infrastructure loan program . According to CMHC&amp;rsquo ; s Loan Commitment Letter , dated Jan. 20 , 2010 , the loan was granted for the development of a solar park . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After the money&amp;nbsp ; was advanced , Blind River received word from Ontario Power Authority that the solar park could not happen due to issues transmitting the power generated by the panels back into the electrical grid . As a result , the municipality moved forward with a number of smaller solar initiatives , 71 in all , totalling about $25 million worth of investments . The remaining money was invested in Plasco. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; CMHC said the town asked to renegotiate its application to reflect an investment in a biomass energy project . CMHC didn&amp;rsquo ; t specify if the town revealed its intentions to invest in Plasco ; however , the federal agency said the revised application met the requirements for funding under the MILP program . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The town says it did inform CMHC of its intention to use the MILP money&amp;nbsp ; to invest in Plasco. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The town and ( North Shore ) needed to invest the funds received from CMHC . BusinessLocal NewsNationalFarm families fight huge legal bill from wind-farm companieshttp : **31;12797;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;12830;TOOLONG ... title= " Shawn Drennan is part of a four-family fight against Ontario 's wind-turbine legislation " alt= " Shawn Drennan is part of a four-family fight against Ontario 's wind-turbine legislation " data-portal-copyright= " Colin Perkel " **28;12866;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 473934 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;By Colin Perkel&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2&gt;TORONTO A demand that four Ontario families pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal costs to billion-dollar companies is a thinly disguised warning to anyone pondering a challenge to industrial wind farms in Ontario , the families say . &lt;/h2&gt; &lt;p&gt; In asking the courts to set the legal bill aside , the citizens say the award would cripple them financially and undermine access to justice , even in important public-interest cases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Court documents show the companies &amp;mdash ; K2 Wind , Armow , and St. Columban &amp;mdash ; are seeking $340,000 in costs from the Drennans , Ryans , Dixons and Kroeplins , who lost their bid to scuttle three wind-farm projects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The families , who worry wind turbines near their homes could harm their health , had challenged the constitutionality of Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s approvals process before Divisional Court . They are now hoping the province&amp;rsquo ; s top court will hear the case , potentially adding more litigation costs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Shawn Drennan said his $240,000 bill was excessive given that he was only looking to protect his rights . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We will have to go to the bank and beg and ask if we can borrow more money to pay their costs and it will be a significant burden on my wife and I , &amp;rdquo ; Shawn Drennan said . &amp;ldquo ; My wife already works two jobs . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s not just a bar to justice ; it&amp;rsquo ; s actually a terror tactic , &amp;rdquo ; lawyer Julian Falconer , who represents the families , said in an interview . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; This is not about money . The idea is to send a message : &amp;lsquo ; We will wipe you out if you challenge us&amp;rsquo ; . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The companies say the high-stakes court challenge forced them to deploy considerable legal resources to defend projects they say are safe . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; While the appellants were entitled to bring their litigation , their decision to do so had significant consequences , &amp;rdquo ; St. Columban argues in its court filing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There must be an appreciation of the real disruption , and real cost , suffered by the adverse party . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Generally speaking , and as a matter of fairness , the losing side in civil proceedings has to pay the legal bills incurred by the winning side . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; K2 , which is putting up 140 turbines , some of which are about 750 metres from the Drennans&amp;rsquo ; home near Goderich , Ont. , on the shore of Lake Huron , says the families knew the risks of losing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In addition , the failed bid to halt construction pending outcome of their court battle was unnecessary and should &amp;ldquo ; never have been brought , &amp;rdquo ; K2 says in its submissions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The families argue they raised an important and novel constitutional issue that is squarely in the public interest given the reasonable prospect of serious harm to the health of citizens . They also say they did not stand to benefit financially . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The companies reject that argument . They maintain the families were indeed fighting a personal battle , do have the means to pay , and say the case was in fact contrary to the public interest because the challenge delayed government-approved green-energy projects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For the families , it&amp;rsquo ; s become a case of &amp;ldquo ; lose your home to save your home , &amp;rdquo ; they say . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; By simply exercising their right to access to the courts , the appellant families now face the disheartening prospect of financial ruin , &amp;rdquo ; their submission states . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When , as in this particular case , the consequence of that access becomes crippling financial loss , &amp;lsquo ; access to justice&amp;rsquo ; becomes a meaningless platitude. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; The Canadian PressMon , 02 Mar 2015 00:50:56 **45;12896;TOOLONG ... servants have 15 million days in banked sick leavehttp : **35;12943;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;12980;TOOLONG ... title= " Ron Cochrane , co-chair of the joint union and management National Joint Council . " alt= " Ron Cochrane , co-chair of the joint union and management National Joint Council . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;13016;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 444328 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s public servants have socked away nearly 15 million days of unused sick leave , which would disappear under the Conservative government&amp;rsquo ; s plan to introduce a new short-term disability plan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That means the 195,330 people who are working today in the core public service &amp;mdash ; those for whom Treasury Board is the employer &amp;mdash ; have banked an average of 75 days , or 15 weeks , of sick leave to fall back on in the event of a prolonged illness . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The size of the sick leave bank was released by Treasury Board in response to an order paper question from&amp;nbsp ; Ottawa South Liberal MP David McGuinty . The statistics show a stockpile of 14.7 million days is what remains after nearly 63,000 people left the core public service over the past six years because they had retired , resigned , were laid off , fired or died . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; ( About 2,600&amp;nbsp ; of those departures were public servants who went to separate agencies such as Canada Revenue Agency or Parks Canada , which are not part of the core public service. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The biggest departures came in the past two years , when more than 25,000 people left jobs in the core public service . The government has backfilled with some new hiring , but overall the core public service has about 22,000 fewer positions now than it did at its peak in 2011 of 217,224. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Public servants can&amp;rsquo ; t cash out their sick leave when they leave government , so those credits disappear and are wiped off the books . With those departures , the amount of banked sick leave sick fell from 16 million days in 2008-09 to about 14.7 million days in 2013-14 . There are about 261 working days in a year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; With the drop in the overall size of the sick leave bank , the average number of sick leave credits per employee also shifted . The average employee had a bank of 76 days in 2008-09 , falling&amp;nbsp ; to 72 days when the 2012 budget cuts began but&amp;nbsp ; increasing to an average 75 days per worker for the past two years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The large number of retirements and resignations over the past six years is&amp;nbsp ; probably older workers who had a stockpile of sick leave credits that would have been cancelled when they left the public service . Any new hires to replace them haven&amp;rsquo ; t started to build their banks . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many predicted there would be a run on the sick leave bank over the past couple of years from disgruntled employees deciding to use some of their sick leave credits before they lost them under the government&amp;rsquo ; s new plan . But nothing in the data suggests that is happening in a significant way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; McGuinty said he was hoping the questions would shed some light on the state of the health of the public service and &amp;ldquo ; what&amp;rsquo ; s going on here&amp;rdquo ; as the government negotiates with the 17 public service unions to reform the way sick leave and disability are managed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We are seeing new forms of psychological distress and serious morale problems that are leading to mental health issues , &amp;rdquo ; said McGuinty. &amp;ldquo ; I rarely come across anyone who says , &amp;lsquo ; I really enjoy what I do in the public service . &amp;rsquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s extremely difficult to get people to talk &amp;hellip ; but it is affecting health , mental health and well-being , and I am trying to get more information on what is going on . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 17 unions argue they have been fighting to get the same kind of information at the bargaining table , where sick leave is the hot negotiating issue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Treasury Board President&amp;nbsp ; Tony Clement wants a new short-term disability plan to replace the existing accumulated sick leave . He argues it would be fairer to all employers while improving the productivity and wellness of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s bureaucrats . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Workplace experts have waded into the debate , arguing that the government should get a handle on the causes of disability in the public service &amp;mdash ; especially for the rising number of mental health claims &amp;mdash ; before re-designing its disability management plans . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They urge the government to adopt the Mental Health Commission&amp;rsquo ; s psychological standard for healthy workplaces , to audit all departments and agencies to determine what working conditions and practices might be behind the high absenteeism and number of mental health claims . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ron Cochrane , the co-chair of the union-management National Joint Council , said Treasury Board negotiators have given the unions basic information about the sick leave usage of their bargaining units but no details by gender , age , years of service or types of illness or disability . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When asked why such drastic changes are required , they don&amp;rsquo ; t even pretend to present a business case for these changes . They simply say it is government policy and proceed to explain how their latest proposal is an improvement on their last , &amp;rdquo ; Cochrane&amp;nbsp ; said . &amp;ldquo ; So it&amp;rsquo ; s pretty hard to engage on this issue when the employer is unable to make a business case for what it is proposing . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The government wants to replace the sick leave provisions in the contracts of all unionized employees that currently give them 15 days of paid sick leave a year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Under the existing regime , public servants can roll over sick days they don&amp;rsquo ; t use from year to year . Those 14.7 million days that are now in the bank are valued at about $4 billion . The government , however , has booked a $1.4-billion liability on that banked leave , based on estimates of how much of those sick leave credits will actually be used . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over a 35-year career , a full-time public servant can earn 525 days in sick leave . Treasury Board says public servants are using an average of 11.5 days of sick leave a year &amp;mdash ; which means the average employee is also banking about 3.5 days a year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The government&amp;rsquo ; s latest proposal introduced a formula that allows employees to convert banked sick leave into credits that could be used to top up disability benefits from 70 per cent of salary to 85 per cent during the first year of the new plan . &amp;nbsp ; The rest of the bank would be abolished in September 2017. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Clement has long argued the existing system was unfair , especially for new employees , because they often don&amp;rsquo ; t have enough sick leave accumulated to bridge the 13 weeks they have to wait to qualify for long-term disability if it is needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The rule of thumb for any employee joining the public service is to save enough sick leave to cover that 13-week waiting period in the event of illness so they can get full pay on sick leave rather than resorting to employment insurance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **29;13046;TOOLONG " **36;13077;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : //Twitter.com/Kathrynmay " &gt;Twit ... &lt;/p&gt; Kathryn May , Ottawa CitizenMon , 02 Feb 2015 15:22:00 **45;13115;TOOLONG ... rate cut surprises markets , puts Tories ' credibility ' at risk'http : **35;13162;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;13199;TOOLONG ... title= " Prime Minister Stephen Harper and Finance Minister Joe Oliver participate in a roundtable discussion at a Canadian Tire Store in Mississauga , Ont. , in December .
