" data-portal-copyright= " Chris Young " **28;13235;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 437847 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Conservative government appears increasingly vulnerable on what is supposed to be its biggest strength &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; economic management &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; after the Bank of Canada lowered its key interest rate Wednesday to try to cushion a faltering Canadian economy from the dramatic fall in oil prices . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finance Minister Joe Oliver again insisted the federal government will balance the books in 2015 , an election year , &amp;nbsp ; but his steadfast position is putting the Conservatives&amp;rsquo ; credibility &amp;ldquo ; severely at risk , &amp;rdquo ; says a former top bureaucrat of Finance Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The opposition NDP and Liberals seized on the Bank of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s gloomy economic assessment as evidence that the Conservative&amp;nbsp ; government&amp;rsquo ; s over-reliance on oil to keep the Canadian economy afloat is bad policy that&amp;rsquo ; s hurting Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Today&amp;rsquo ; s rate cut shows that the Bank of Canada believes that the trouble facing our economy is greater than the Conservatives are willing to admit , &amp;rdquo ; NDP Leader Tom Mulcair&amp;nbsp ; said&amp;nbsp ; in Toronto . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s high time that Stephen Harper stopped hiding , stopped hiding his finance minister , stopped playing peek-a-boo with the budget date . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In reducing its key overnight rate to 0.75 per cent from one per cent &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; the first change since September 2010 &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; the Bank of Canada sent shock waves through the markets , while its downgrade to growth forecasts and concerns about the economy sent further ripples through federal political circles . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The central bank , in its new monetary policy report , said the drop in oil prices &amp;ldquo ; will be unambiguously negative for the Canadian economy in 2015 and subsequent years . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The bank is assuming oil prices of $60 US per barrel for the next two years &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; far below the more than $80 US that Oliver and the Conservative government used for their most recent fiscal assumptions , which predicted a return to surplus in 2015-16. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Oliver , who has delayed the federal budget until at least April due to the volatility in oil prices , maintained Wednesday that the government will return to surplus this year , despite the bank&amp;rsquo ; s gloomier outlook . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We will not comment directly on interest rate decisions that are the responsibility of the Bank of Canada , &amp;rdquo ; he&amp;nbsp ; said in an emailed statement . &amp;ldquo ; As we&amp;rsquo ; ve always said , Canada is not immune to the economic challenges and decisions made beyond our borders . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In an interview with CNBC at the World Economic Forum in Davos , Switzerland , Oliver said the Canadian economy &amp;ldquo ; is doing quite well . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A balanced budget is very important and it&amp;rsquo ; s something we&amp;rsquo ; ve been promising Canadians since the depths of the recession , &amp;rdquo ; Oliver said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Scott Clark , an adjunct professor at Carleton University and former deputy minister of Finance Canada , said the government is now &amp;ldquo ; caught in a corner of their own making&amp;rdquo ; by promising billions in tax breaks and a balanced budget when the dollars likely aren&amp;rsquo ; t there to afford all of this . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Their credibility is taking a beating because people are saying , &amp;lsquo ; This doesn&amp;rsquo ; t add up , &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; Clark said in an interview . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Clark said he doesn&amp;rsquo ; t see how the government will be able to afford the billions in family tax breaks and still balance the books in 2015-16 . From an economic perspective , he doesn&amp;rsquo ; t think it&amp;rsquo ; s a big deal if the government has to run a small deficit . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They see sound economic policy entirely in the world of &amp;lsquo ; eliminate the deficit&amp;rsquo ; &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; that&amp;rsquo ; s how they define their brand , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; They now know that&amp;rsquo ; s a corner which is hard to get out of . If they were smart , they would just accept reality . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Bank of Canada Governor Stephen Poloz noted the Canadian economy will suffer from lower crude prices because income from oil exports will fall , while investment and jobs in the oil patch are already being slashed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While lower interest rates will see some Canadians take on more household debt , the rate cut will also help cushion the economic blow from loss of income and jobs caused by lower oil prices , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re taking out an insurance policy against risks , &amp;rdquo ; Poloz told reporters in Ottawa . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This slowing ( of growth ) is pretty significant . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Poloz said there will be some partial offsets , such as&amp;nbsp ; Canadians saving on fuel costs and spending some of that money elsewhere , as well as a stronger U.S. economy &amp;ndash ; &amp;nbsp ; combined with a lower loonie&amp;nbsp ; &amp;ndash ; likely boosting Canadian exports . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The central bank&amp;rsquo ; s report is the latest in a series of deteriorating economic forecasts over the last week . TD Bank has warned that the Conservative government could run a deficit in 2015-16. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Conference Board of Canada said this week the plunge in oil prices is expected to cut $4.3 billion from federal revenues this year , a blow to a government whose new family tax cuts are expected to cost $4.6 billion in 2015-16. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau said Wednesday the bank&amp;rsquo ; s poor economic outlook underscores the need for strong leadership from the federal government . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Unfortunately , this is a government that has put all its eggs in one basket with high oil prices and now doesn&amp;rsquo ; t have a plan , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Trudeau would not comment on whether the government should abandon its plans to produce a balanced budget and instead run a deficit , given the bank&amp;rsquo ; s projections . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , he again attacked the Conservatives&amp;rsquo ; income-splitting plan , which he said will give a $2-billion tax break to the wealthiest 15 per cent of Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s simply not responsible and that&amp;rsquo ; s the first thing to take off the table , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt; -- With files from Lee Berthiaume , Ottawa Citizen . &lt;/em&gt; NewsCanada imposes new sanctions as Russia 's economy teetershttp : **33;14060;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;14095;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;14131;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 416221 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada is joining its allies in tightening the screws on Russian President Vladimir Putin , with new trade sanctions&amp;nbsp ; meant&amp;nbsp ; to put further pressure on Russia&amp;rsquo ; s teetering economy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The new measures are in retaliation for Russia&amp;rsquo ; s annexation of Crimea and its support for separatist rebels in eastern Ukraine . The measures&amp;nbsp ; target 20 Russians and separatist Ukrainian leaders , and prohibit the import of certain goods from Russia&amp;rsquo ; s oil and gas sector . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The move comes days after the European Union and the U.S. also imposed additional trade restrictions against Russia , whose energy-dependent economy has been hit hard by the falling price of oil . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Foreign Affairs Minister John Baird announced&amp;nbsp ; the new sanctions in a press conference Friday , saying it is up to Putin to reverse course on Ukraine if he wants to end the pain that is being done to his country&amp;rsquo ; s economy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This much is clear : Russians are paying for their leader&amp;rsquo ; s reckless aggression , &amp;rdquo ; Baird said . &amp;ldquo ; The ruble&amp;rsquo ; s dive should be enough to give President Putin and his backers pause . If he wants to turn his economy , he must pull out of Ukraine and he must return Crimea . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Putin appeared defiant in a three-hour news conference on Thursday , even though Russia&amp;rsquo ; s currency , the ruble , has lost about half its value this year and the central bank hiked interest rates 6.5 per cent to 17 per cent on Tuesday . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Russian president predicted the country would emerge from the economic crisis in about two years . He denied that his foreign policy was responsible for the problems , and instead blamed the West for trying to weaken Russia . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Baird was asked whether imposing additional sanctions at a time when Russia&amp;rsquo ; s economy is in trouble could provoke even more aggressive action . He noted the Russian military&amp;rsquo ; s continuing presence in parts of Georgia and Moldova years after conflicts with those two countries . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Being unforceful hasn&amp;rsquo ; t worked , &amp;rdquo ; he said in reference to those disputes . &amp;ldquo ; I think this is the right path as well as the diplomatic isolation that the Russian leadership and those close to them are facing . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In addition to sanctions , Canada has suspended military co-operation with Russia as well as economic and diplomatic discussions in retaliation for its role in the crisis in Ukraine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Baird said sanctions can have the desired effect , even if they don&amp;rsquo ; t always work as quickly as some would hope . We&amp;rsquo ; re always looking at what more we can do . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **36;14161;TOOLONG " **53;14199;TOOLONG &lt;a href= " http : **27;14254;TOOLONG " target= " blank " **29;14283;TOOLONG &; ... &lt;/p&gt; Lee Berthiaume , Ottawa CitizenSat , 20 Dec 2014 18:15:48 **45;14314;TOOLONG ... Granatstein : Low oil prices are part of a Saudi long gamehttp : **36;14361;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;14399;TOOLONG ... title= " A Suncor oil sands facility is pictured near Fort McMurray , Alta. , on July 10 , 2012. " alt= " A Suncor oil sands facility is pictured near Fort McMurray , Alta. , on July 10 , 2012. " data-portal-copyright= " Jeff McIntosh " **28;14435;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 409519 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; How does a manufacturer beat down his competitors ? Flood the market with goods and sell them at a low price , hoping to drive competitors into the ground . That , in essence , is what Saudi Arabia is doing with its recent tactics with its oil . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the last few weeks , the Saudis refused to agree to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries ( OPEC ) cutting production as a way of dealing with an oil glut and falling prices . Then several&amp;nbsp ; days ago , the Saudis&amp;rsquo ; state-owned oil company cut the price it charges for oil sales to Asia and the United States . These moves amount to classic cutthroat market tactics . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But there is more going on here . The Saudis are launching a pre-emptive strike at shale oil and oil sands production , in effect striking at Canada , the United States , and the European countries now seeking shale oil . Production from these unconventional sources is expensive , many fields requiring oil to sell for $100 a barrel to be economic . But the Saudis have successfully connived to drive the price of a barrel of oil down to the low-$60s , and they have indicated that they do not expect the price to stabilize until it reaches $60 a barrel . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Oil at that low price does not mean that the oil sands will stop producing , but it does strongly suggest that exploration and drilling here will decline substantially and that investors will back away before sinking hard cash into new ventures . The recent rout on Canadian stock markets , the hammering that our oil giants have taken , will likely continue . The same difficulties apply in spades to shale oil producers , drillers , and investors , and estimates are that American shale oil production will drop by a third . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The lower prices at the pump are good for motorists , to be sure . But they are also manna from heaven for the environmentalists hoping to strangle the oilsands and shale oil production , along with pipeline projects . The opposition to such projects has been heartened , and Naomi Klein , the goddess of the anti-capitalist set , is already issuing pronunciamentos proclaiming coming victories . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The declining price of oil will hit Alberta and Canada hard , and the budget surpluses Finance minister Joe Oliver saw coming just a few weeks ago now seem chimerical . In late November , Premier Jim Prentice seemed to have everything under control , but no longer . Other nations will be hammered even harder &amp;mdash ; Iran , Nigeria , and Venezuela especially . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But so will Vladimir Putin&amp;rsquo ; s Russia . His economy was doing well when oil was priced above $100 a barrel . But with the massive cut in oil prices and with Western sanctions because of his incursions into Ukraine starting to bite , Putin&amp;rsquo ; s oligarchs are hurting and so are Russian state revenues . The ruble has plunged dramatically , and $1 Canadian today will buy almost 50 rubles . The NATO countries are not immune to the effects of the oil price drop , but compared to Moscow , they are and will remain in much better shape . President Obama , good environmentalist that he is , will worry about cheaper oil putting more cars on the road , but he will not be upset to see Putin&amp;rsquo ; s Russia in deeper economic trouble . The domestic pressures are almost certain to force Putin to re-think his tactics and probably to put his aggressive moves on hold &amp;mdash ; for a time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As for the Saudis , they sit firmly in the catbird seat . They can produce their oil cheaply , and they can keep pumping forever at the current low price . But like every other producer who starts a price war , the rich sheiks in Riyadh will choose their time to jack their oil prices back up . That time will come when the oilsands development has stalled , the pipeline projects have run into even more difficulty , and new shale oil projects have ground to a halt . Cheap oil serves the Saudi purpose for now . But the longer game , as always , is for higher prices . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **27;14465;TOOLONG . **26;14494;TOOLONG is a Fellow of the Canadian Defence and Foreign Affairs Institute . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; J.L. GranatsteinFri , 12 Dec 2014 16:48:31 **45;14522;TOOLONG ... Rivers : Are low oil prices good for the environment ? http : **28;14569;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;14599;TOOLONG ... title= " Regular gas was 99.9 cents a litre in November at the COSTCO in Ottawa . " alt= " Regular gas was 99.9 cents a litre in November at the COSTCO in Ottawa . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;14635;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 409572 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The price of oil has fallen by almost half in the last six months . This affects both our transport choices as well as investments in oil extraction , so it is difficult to pin down exactly what the effect is on greenhouse gas emissions . World leaders met in Lima this week to negotiate an agreement on climate change ; it is important to consider what effect the major slump in world oil prices over the last six months has on the environment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Recent history provides some clues . The long surge in the &lt;a href= " https : **32;14665;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;&lt;span style= " **25;14699;TOOLONG ; " &gt;price of **28;14726;TOOLONG oil from around $20 per barrel at the beginning of the millennium to a high of almost $150 per barrel in 2008 brought about fundamental changes in energy markets . Car companies made significant investments in alternative drive trains , such that fuel-sipping hybrid vehicles now make up a small but growing share of vehicles , and such that the fuel efficiency of the entire new vehicle stock is poised to reach double today&amp;rsquo ; s level within a decade . Last year , Tesla&amp;rsquo ; s elegant new sedan was the first ever electric vehicle to be universally praised as the &lt;a href= " http : **34;14756;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;&lt;span style= " **25;14792;TOOLONG ; " &gt;car of the **27;14819;TOOLONG , and a wave of similar vehicles from other companies is likely to carve out an important niche in the car market of tomorrow . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the supply side , the high price of oil during the last decade has led to a frantic search for alternative sources . This has fuelled expansion in the Canadian oil sands , which are among the highest cost sources of oil worldwide , requiring relatively high prices to remain profitable . It has also provided the impetus for the technology investments underlying the shale boom currently underway in the United States , which has transformed world energy markets . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The price of oil affects not just technology , but also behaviour . After rising every year since 1960 ( when the U.S. Bureau of Transport started collecting data ) , the distance driven by U.S. passengers has&amp;nbsp ; &lt;a href= " https : **31;14848;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;&lt;span style= " **25;14881;TOOLONG ; " &gt;fallen every **27;14908;TOOLONG since about 2008 , driven in part by high fuel prices . And high fuel prices have even motivated people to move out of car-centric suburbs and into city centres . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Clearly , these major changes in technology and behaviour affect not only our economy , but also the environment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Similarly , when the world price of oil drops as it has over the past months , there are a number of impacts for a country like Canada , each of which can have implications for greenhouse gas emissions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The obvious effect of a big swing in oil prices is its effect on gasoline prices , and on our resulting demand . Crude oil accounts for about half of the price of gasoline at the pump , and a portion of the tax on gasoline is dependent on its price , so a 40 per cent drop in crude oil prices &amp;mdash ; as occurred over the last few months &amp;mdash ; results in roughly a 25 per cent drop in the retail price of gasoline . This has predictable impacts on consumer demand : when prices drop we buy larger and less fuel efficient vehicles , and we drive them more . &amp;nbsp ; As a result , our consumption of gasoline increases . &amp;nbsp ; Estimates from economists suggest that a 25 percent drop in gasoline price likely increases gasoline consumption by around 2 to 5 per cent immediately , and by 10 to 20 percent over the longer term . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Aside from this obvious effect , there are a number of other more subtle effects . For an oil-exporting country like Canada , a big drop in oil prices results in a significant weakening of purchasing power . Lower income means less consumption , and less emissions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Lower oil prices also discourage new exploration and investment in oil and gas projects , especially in high cost regions like Canada&amp;rsquo ; s oil sands . Since oil sands represent Canada&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;a href= " http : **34;14937;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;fastest-growing source of emissions&lt;/a&gt; , reducing expansion in the oil sands has obvious implications for emissions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finally , just as high oil prices over the past decade have fuelled a search for alternative technologies that can displace oil , a sustained period of low oil prices will dampen investment in alternative technologies . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The net impact of these and other more subtle effects is not immediately clear . However , Environment Canada&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;a href= " http : **34;14973;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;recent report&lt;/a&gt; on Canada&amp;rsquo ; s emissions provides an estimate of the overall effect of sustained changes in world energy prices on Canadian emissions . They estimate that a sustained fall in oil price from $102 to $70 per barrel ( along with a similar fall in natural gas prices ) is likely to have a negligible overall effect on Canada&amp;rsquo ; s emissions by 2020 , changing overall emissions by much less than one per cent . In their model , increased emissions from driving are cancelled out by reduced emissions from oil and gas operations . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As a result , even if oil prices remain at today&amp;rsquo ; s levels for a prolonged period , Canada is unlikely to meet its international commitments to reduce greenhouse gases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is , however , one important avenue through which oil prices can affect the environment that is perhaps more important . Low oil prices may make it more politically feasible to implement the type of carbon pricing reforms that are considered necessary for significantly reducing emissions . A modest carbon tax , as implemented in British Columbia , or cap and trade system , as in Quebec , would increase the price of gasoline , but by an amount much smaller than that caused by the recent drop in oil prices . Consumers may more readily accept such a policy at a time when gasoline prices are low than when they are already high . If so , a period of low oil prices could be more environmentally transformative than commonly thought . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **27;15009;TOOLONG Rivers&lt;/strong&gt; is the Canada Research Chair in Climate and Energy Policy at the University of Ottawa . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Nic RiversFri , 12 Dec 2014 16:45:59 **45;15038;TOOLONG ... He&amp;rsquo ; s not a demonstrative man but a little crinkling around the eyes may have been from joy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As&amp;nbsp ; with Couillard , Wynne&amp;rsquo ; s meeting with Prentice produced a lot of talk about working together on national issues . &amp;ldquo ; This is a very important nation-building project , &amp;rdquo ; Prentice said , emphasizing the number of Ontario companies ( 1,100 , by his count ) that make parts and machinery used in the oilsands . The pipeline would&amp;nbsp ; mean new jobs everywhere along its route , said the Alberta premier , a Tory and former Stephen Harper cabinet minister . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Wynne , the Liberal , made a similar argument about the environment . &amp;nbsp ; Alberta charges a&amp;nbsp ; greenhouse-gas tax on large emitters ( though it&amp;rsquo ; s small and under review ) and Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s still thinking about the idea . Ontario has eliminated its coal-fired electricity plants , while coal still supplies more than half of Alberta&amp;rsquo ; s power . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; We all have to do our part and it will look different depending where we are in the country , &amp;rdquo ; Wynne&amp;nbsp ; said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two different national projects , but both being pushed by premiers , not the feds. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As for the pipeline , TransCanada only filed its formal , 30,000-page application at the end of October and a review is likely to take more than&amp;nbsp ; a year . " data-portal-copyright= " JOSE JORDAN " **28;15705;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 223054 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; A new report from the Fraser Institute is&amp;nbsp ; providing wind for the sails of Ontario renewable energy opponents by suggesting that the province&amp;rsquo ; s&amp;nbsp ; rising energy prices are largely a result of investments into wind and solar generation . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The report , released Thursday , says&amp;nbsp ; wind and solar production accounts for just four per cent of the province&amp;rsquo ; s energy needs but is&amp;nbsp ; responsible for 20 per cent of all energy costs paid by Ontarians. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And even with that imbalance , &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; the government wants to triple the number of wind and solar generators , &amp;rdquo ; said Tom Adams , independent energy analyst and co-author of the Fraser Institute report . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In the U.S. power rates have been falling , but Ontarians are paying more than ever , &amp;rdquo ; Adams added . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Since its introduction in 2009 , Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s Green Energy Act has been a lightning rod for controversy . The act sets a priority on renewable energy&amp;nbsp ; technologies and offers high-paying incentives to organizations willing to set up solar , wind and other renewable energy-producing sources . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Prices , meantime , have continued to march upward . According to the Ontario Energy Board , which regulates utilities , consumers were paying 4 cents per kilowatt hour ( kWh ) during off-peak hours in November 2008 , four months before the Green Energy Act was implemented . Those same consumers now pay 7.7 cents per kWh . Peak-hours costs have climbed from 8.8 cents per kWh in November 2008 to 14 cents today . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over the same period , the province&amp;rsquo ; s energy use has remained relatively stable . According to the Independent Electricity System Operator , the organization responsible for connecting and monitoring all of Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s various power grids and predicting demand for electricity , the total demand in Ontario in 2009 was 139 terawatt-hours ( a terawatt is equal to 1 trillion watts ) . In 2013 , demand had&amp;nbsp ; increased by 1.22 per cent to 140.7 terawatt-hours. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;15735;TOOLONG ... title= " No caption , leave this text or replace image " alt= " No caption , leave this text or replace image " data-portal-copyright= " DENNIS LEUNG " **28;15771;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 371747 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Over the past decade , electricity prices in Ontario have skyrocketed and they&amp;rsquo ; ll continue to rise unless the province puts the interests of ordinary Ontarians ahead of industry insiders , &amp;rdquo ; said Ross McKitrick , a senior fellow at the Fraser Institute and economics professor at the University of Guelph. &amp;ldquo ; Many European countries made costly commitments to renewable energy but are now winding back those commitments . If Ontario wants to provide residents and businesses with relief from rising power costs , it should reconsider costly commitments made to renewable energy companies . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 40-page report suggests reopening four of Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s 12 coal-fired generating plants , which are equipped with advanced air pollution control technologies , to generate cheaper energy until the province&amp;rsquo ; s nuclear facilities can be refurbished . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Reverting to coal-fired energy is becoming popular . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Germany , which has been at the forefront of investments into green energy , announced early this year that it would reactivate a number of plants and increase coal-generation&amp;nbsp ; production to the highest level of more than a decade . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jennifer Beaudry , a spokeswoman for the Ministry of Energy , quickly squashed the idea of Ontario doing the same . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This year , Ontario became the first jurisdiction in North America to eliminate coal as a source of electricity production , &amp;rdquo ; she said in a prepared statement . &amp;ldquo ; Replacing coal-fired electricity generation was the single largest climate change initiative undertaken in North America . Altogether , more than 85 per cent of the power generated in Ontario during 2013 came from emissions-free sources of energy such as water , nuclear and renewables. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Beaudry took issue with the Fraser Institute&amp;rsquo ; s figures , maintaining that wind and solar generation account for eight per cent , not 20 per cent , of consumers&amp;rsquo ; bills . The institute&amp;rsquo ; s&amp;nbsp ; Adams argued that the ministry&amp;rsquo ; s estimates leave out numerous factors , including selling excess power at a loss to neighbouring provinces and states . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ontario Power Authority , responsible for planning Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s various electricity systems , refused to comment on the report . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other research supports the report&amp;rsquo ; s premise that the province is becoming less competitive compared to other jurisdictions in North America . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to an annual report from&amp;nbsp ; Hydro-Qu&amp;eacute ; bec , which tracks the price of electricity across much of the continent , power bills in Ottawa and Toronto ranked 14th and 15th highest among 22 major cities in Canada and the U.S. Average prices of 13.45 cents per kWh in Ottawa and 13.78 cents in Toronto compare with 7.06 cents in Montreal , 9.71 cents in Vancouver and 11.61 cents in Chicago . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The most expensive was New York City , where residents pay an average of 21.25 cents per kWh. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Fraser Institute has long been lobbying against the government&amp;rsquo ; s green energy plans . A report issued by the institute on Oct. 22 argued that Ontario&amp;nbsp ; can cancel or change contracts it has signed with energy producers by changing legislation pertaining to energy production . The &amp;ldquo ; ATIP&amp;rdquo ; &amp;nbsp ; records detail painstaking attempts by these well-meaning Environment Canada employees to make sure the public was well-informed about the ice melt , and to see that the&amp;nbsp ; federal government&amp;nbsp ; wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t be left in the shadows of frequent U.S. federal government briefings on the same issue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The documents contain emails , drafts of media messaging&amp;nbsp ; and attempts to get permissions up and down the federal food chain to set a date for a&amp;nbsp ; briefing ( nine levels of permissions were needed ) . The&amp;nbsp ; records&amp;nbsp ; cover a period of about four weeks . But no briefing ever happened , and the hundreds of pages of records don&amp;rsquo ; t explain why . Meanwhile , Canadian journalists sought and quoted U.S. government experts on the Arctic issue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The failure to approve even a technical&amp;nbsp ; briefing appears to feed&amp;nbsp ; the fears of those who think the federal government is &amp;ldquo ; muzzling&amp;rdquo ; its own scientists , and some experts&amp;nbsp ; made this point to Munro . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Citizen asked Environment Canada by phone ( actually , I&amp;nbsp ; had to leave a message ) and&amp;nbsp ; in writing Monday morning to respond and for some information about why the briefing was cancelled . I&amp;nbsp ; didn&amp;rsquo ; t get a response that day . Prodded&amp;nbsp ; again Tuesday , after Munro&amp;rsquo ; s article had run , the department sent an email with its response . &amp;nbsp ; Here&amp;rsquo ; s what I&amp;nbsp ; asked , and what the written response&amp;nbsp ; was . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Question : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;em&gt;It appears several public servants worked on the information for a media briefing on the low Arctic ice levels , that they worked on it for several weeks , and that they communicated to all the right people in the department that they were preparing it . Yet in the end the briefing was never held . Why was it cancelled ? &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Question : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;em&gt;According to the atip documents , nine levels of approval were needed , from the Canadian Ice Service right up to the minister 's office and PCO . Why were nine levels of approval needed ? &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Answer from Environment Canada : &lt;/strong&gt; All of Environment Canada&amp;rsquo ; s findings were released to the public on the departmental website . It was felt that a media technical briefing was no longer needed . Communications protocol requires certain levels of approval for most media events to ensure high quality information and that senior decision making levels are aware . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Question : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;em&gt;Some critics have said the cancelling of the briefing on such a major environmental phenomenon is evidence -- in their eyes , further evidence -- that the Conservative government is silencing scientists . Would you respond to this accusation ? &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Answer from Environment Canada : &lt;/strong&gt; Since 2006 , the Government of Canada has invested over $4 billion in science and technology at Environment Canada alone . Thanks to these investments , Canada is world renowned for producing ground breaking research that benefits Canadians and the environment . In fact , since 2006 , Environment Canada has produced or contributed to almost 5000 studies and scientific articles . These contributions are world-class and are cited 40% more often than the world average . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Environment Canada&amp;rsquo ; s response to media inquiries is strong . In 2013 , Environment Canada responded to more than 2,500 media calls . Media Relations staff facilitates approximately 1,000 media interviews , as well as providing written responses to media questions . The number of total interviews processed by media relations is lower than last year as , for climatology questions , most media outlets now go directly to EC&amp;rsquo ; s senior for climatologist , David Phillips rather than through media relations . David Phillips completed an estimated additional 1,000 interviews last year related to climatology. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The above totals do not include the approximately 5,000 media calls received each year by our Warning Preparedness Meteorologists at their dedicated 1-866 severe weather media access line . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Question : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;em&gt;Will Environment Canada permit the Canadian Ice Service to hold media briefings in future if major environmental developments occur ? &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Answer from Environment Canada : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;nbsp ; The department reviews daily the need to communicate extreme weather phenomena to Canadians and holds media briefings and individual interviews on a regular basis to help keep Canadians and our maritime community safe and informed . For example , on July 3 , 2014 , officials from Environment Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Canadian Hurricane Centre did a media technical briefing concerning Hurricane Arthur . Media briefings and interviews will continue to take place as needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The emailed response was signed by one Laura Lauzon , presumably of Environment Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The prime minister embarks Wednesday on his annual Arctic trip . On the side , not far from the house , they run Derks Elevator Inc. , which stores and dries soybean for area producers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the afternoon of June 2 , in a 66-by-40-foot building that houses an industrial bean roaster , fire broke out . When it was finally extinguished , 10 hours later , the building and contents were a wreck . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After 27 years , they would have to rebuild the business . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hydro One soon showed up to tag the pole that fed the building and ensure the supply to the house , on a separate meter , was operating properly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The roaster building , says Derks , had its own &amp;ldquo ; smart meter&amp;rdquo ; , which bills the customer at different rates according to the time of day when the electricity is consumed . ( They&amp;rsquo ; re usually called time-of-use meters. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Along comes a bill in July . It says&amp;nbsp ; an estimate was taken on June 3 and another on July 4 , though the word &amp;ldquo ; estimate&amp;rdquo ; was in fine print and easy to miss . The readings calculated that 6,125&amp;nbsp ; kilowatt-hours of power had been consumed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because the meter is so &amp;ldquo ; smart&amp;rdquo ; , it actually broke down the estimated hours into on-peak ( 2,112 ) , mid-peak ( 1,382 ) and off-peak ( 2,630 ) and came up with a total bill of $1,214 . In that total was a &amp;ldquo ; delivery charge&amp;rdquo ; of $412. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Note the dates : Billing began on June 3 , which creates a slight problem . The building was a pile of ash on June 2 . It could not have used a single watt&amp;nbsp ; of power . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve never trusted these automatic readings , &amp;rdquo ; says Derks , who was upset enough to go public and appeal to opposition MPP Randy Hillier , a vocal Hydro critic . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A lot of people in the country don&amp;rsquo ; t. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When he called Hydro One to complain , he said he got nowhere . A Hydro One official explained that the smart meter goes into estimate mode as a default when the meter is no longer communicating with the network . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is what happened when the fire occurred . It billed him based on previous monthly consumption , blind to the news of the fire . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Derks said he was called by Hydro on Thursday and told the $1,214 bill , which he paid , will be refunded . The new bill is in the $50 range , as he is still required to pay a portion of the delivery charge . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t listen to me until ( the Citizen ) got involved . I guess they figured I was just a dumb farmer . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hillier , meanwhile , says a recurring theme in the hundreds of complaints he&amp;rsquo ; s received is whether the time-of-use meters are , firstly , measuring consumption properly , and , secondly , transferring that information smoothly to Hydro One&amp;rsquo ; s digital brain for accurate billing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hydro One has admitted to a relatively small number of wireless communication problems with its 1.3 million&amp;nbsp ; smart meters , which it says are subject to rigorous testing and work properly 99.9 per cent of the time . ( Heavy forest , for instance , can foul up the wireless signals. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hillier doesn&amp;rsquo ; t buy it . @@31978392 <p> Ottawa Citizen - RSS Feedhttps : **28;17807;TOOLONG , 21 Jul 2020 23:32:55 +0000uOttawa team examines effects of oral contraceptives on brain developmenthttps : **28;17837;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;17867;TOOLONG ... title= " Prof. Nafissa Ismail poses for a photo at her home in Gatineau . Nafissa is one of the authors of a new study looking at how the use of oral contraceptives affects women during puberty and adolescence . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;17903;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1679151 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;17933;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Women who start using oral contraceptives during puberty or adolescence may not respond to stress as well as their counterparts who begin using birth-control pills as adults , or not at all , according to research done by the University of Ottawa . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Additionally , the study of 75 women suggests that early use of birth control pills may contribute to the development of mood-related disorders , such as depression . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nafissa Ismail , associate psychology professor and uOttawa research chair in stress and mental health , and Dr. Andra Smith , uOttawa psychology professor , are leading a research team headed by graduate student Rupali Sharma . Their goal is to determine how the synthetic hormones in birth control pills affect women&amp;rsquo ; s health , particularly in young women whose brains are still in critical stages of development . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Using stress tests and magnetic resonance imaging , their research shows that women who use oral contraceptives displayed greater activity in their prefrontal cortices when performing memory tasks . The implication of this increased activity , Ismail says , needs further investigation , but it may suggest that their brains simply have to work harder to arrive at the same outcomes as women who aren&amp;rsquo ; t on the pill . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The results of the first phase of their research are now being published in the journal Hormones and Behavior. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the dulled response to social stress is of concern , she adds , because it suggests that the brains of early users of the pill have developed in ways that don&amp;rsquo ; t properly react to stress and thus never resolve it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The women who started contraception during puberty don&amp;rsquo ; t show that stress response that they should when they&amp;rsquo ; re presented with a stressor , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; And that is worrisome because that means that , first , they&amp;rsquo ; re not reacting to the stressor , and secondly , they&amp;rsquo ; re not bringing their system back to homeostasis . So subjectively , they&amp;rsquo ; re telling us that they&amp;rsquo ; re stressed , but their body is not reacting to it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And while any definitive causal relationship remains inconclusive , and women who were diagnosed with mental-health issues were excluded from the study , Ismail notes that a blunted stress response is common in women who are suffering from depression . &amp;ldquo ; It points to a mechanism that could explain why many women suffer depression once they start oral contraceptives. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Relatively little research has been devoted to the effects of oral contraceptives on neural development , despite the six decades that have passed since the pill came on the market . &amp;ldquo ; Women&amp;rsquo ; s health research has been lacking because we&amp;rsquo ; ve given priority to issues related more to men&amp;rsquo ; s health , or those affecting most of the population , and we&amp;rsquo ; ve kind of forgotten that 50 per cent of the population has unique problems , &amp;rdquo ; says Ismail . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But it&amp;rsquo ; s worth investigation , and it needs investigation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Oral contraceptives , which inhibit ovulation , help prevent sperm from entering the fallopian tubes and deter any fertilized eggs from attaching to the uterine wall , are used by an estimated 150 million women . They are also prescribed to young women to combat acne problems , heavy menstrual flow and pre-menstrual syndrome . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We want to find out the impact that it has on these young women , too , &amp;rdquo ; says Ismail . &amp;ldquo ; And we want to find the mechanism that would help us understand why some women are more susceptible than others to developing mood disorders , and whether the birth-control pill is a contributing factor , and if there is any way to predict , before a woman even starts to take the pill , whether it will be the right fit for her , or if there might be injuring consequences that we could prevent by using an alternate method . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We don&amp;rsquo ; t want to discourage women or girls from taking oral contraceptives , &amp;rdquo ; she adds . &amp;ldquo ; We just want them to be informed , to be able to weigh the pros and cons , and then make an informed decision . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **30;17969;TOOLONG " **37;18001;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; Bruce DeachmanTue , 21 Jul 2020 23:32:55 **45;18040;TOOLONG ... Scientists have looked at these five treatmentshttp : **30;18745;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;18777;TOOLONG ... title= " " Gene Editing . " " alt= " " Gene Editing . " " data-portal-copyright= " Mike Faille " **28;18813;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1546798 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Scientists have been researching ways to increase a human&amp;rsquo ; s healthspan &amp;mdash ; and possible lifespan &amp;mdash ; for decades . Here are things they have considered , and what they have learned . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The intervention : &lt;/strong&gt; Rapamycin &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt; What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; First identified in the 1970s in a soil sample from Easter Island , this FDA-approved drug is used to suppress the immune system in transplant patients . Counterintuitively , it also appears to boost immune function in healthy animals . Rapamycin may reduce inflammation , which increases with age . One study found that rapamycin rejuvenated the hearts of old mice . After treatment , there were significant improvements to cardiac function . Research with mice has also found that even when they where administered rapamycin late in life , the mice still had improvements to lifespan and their healthspan. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The verdict : &lt;/strong&gt; Geroscientist Matt Kaeberlein said rapamycin shows the most promise of any drug that targets aging , in his opinion , although he doesn&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily think rapamycin will increase lifespan by 20 to 30 years on average in people . &amp;ldquo ; Although it might at the right dose . I do think there&amp;rsquo ; s reason to believe that rapamycin could improve several age-related health problems , including boosting immune function and protecting against dementia , cancers , and heart disease . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But critics say it is unclear what the downstream effects could be . &amp;ldquo ; If you take a compound like that for a few decades , there may be downstream effect&amp;nbsp ; &amp;mdash ; a small epidemic of lymphoma , perhaps , &amp;rdquo ; said geriatrician Dr. Peter Boling . While it is approved to prevent rejection in organ transplant patients , it is not approved to treat aging . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are also questions about side effects , which may include susceptibility to infection and the possibility of developing lymphoma. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We still don&amp;rsquo ; t know about all of the hidden dangers . As hopeful as we might be , we have to be aware of the limitations , &amp;rdquo ; said Boling. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The intervention : &lt;/strong&gt; Metformin &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; This drug has been prescribed to millions of people to treat diabetes . Among other effects , it decreases insulin levels . It also appears to target biological mechanisms related to aging . Its anti-aging effects may be linked to its influences on metabolic and cellular processes associated with inflammation . It has been linked to lifespan extension and protection against age-related diseases in animal models . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The verdict : &lt;/strong&gt; The speculation in scientific circles has been that many of the drugs used to treat early-stage chronic disease may be effective , at least in part , because they target aging itself . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Metformin is an interesting case , &amp;rdquo ; said Kaeberlein . It clearly increases survival in people with diabetes and likely would do the same for pre-diabetics and others with significant metabolic disease , which represents a growing percentage of adults , he said . However , it&amp;rsquo ; s less clear whether metformin will be beneficial in people who are metabolically healthy and exercise regularly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The studies in mice suggest that metformin is different from rapamycin , in the sense that metformin only increases lifespan by a very small amount and in some cases has been reported to have no effect or even shortens lifespan in mice . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The FDA has accepted a clinical trial , Targeting Aging with Metformin , known as TAME , which will test whether metformin can delay the onset of age-related diseases and conditions including cancer , cardiovascular disease and Alzheimer&amp;rsquo ; s disease . The goal of the trial , which is estimated to cost $55 million , is not to help people live to be 120 years old but &amp;ldquo ; to add health to our years , &amp;rdquo ; said the American Federation for Aging Research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Like metformin , several promising drugs show great potential and await trials . If successful , the TAME trial would give the pharmaceutical industry impetus to advance these drugs and transform aging from a period of sickness to a time of extended vitality . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The intervention : &lt;/strong&gt; Caloric restriction &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; A dietary regimen that reduces calories while maintaining nutrients . Research in lab animals , which started almost a century ago , has shown that it is possible to delay age-related diseases in mice and rats through dietary and caloric restriction , but results have varied . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A parallel study of two groups of rhesus monkeys , one at the University of Wisconsin and the other at the U.S. National Institute on Aging , looked at the life-prolonging and health effects of a calorie-restricted diet . The researchers found that the Wisconsin monkeys on a diet with 30 per cent fewer calories than the control group survived to about 28 years for males and about 30 years for females &amp;mdash ; a couple of years above average for monkeys in captivity . Calorie-restricted monkeys in both groups showed fewer age-related health conditions compared to the control monkeys . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some &amp;ldquo ; biohackers&amp;rdquo ; &amp;mdash ; people who use biological interventions to optimize health &amp;mdash ; have embarked on caloric restriction diets , with the goal of living longer . Entrepreneur Dave Asprey , author of Bulletproof Diet , has said he plans to live to be 180 and is hacking his own biology with a number of interventions , including supplements and a strict diet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The verdict so far : &lt;/strong&gt; The rhesus monkey study also produced some contradictory findings . The National Institute on Aging&amp;rsquo ; s study found that while the dieting monkeys showed improved health , they didn&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily live longer than the control monkeys . It&amp;rsquo ; s not clear why there was a difference between the two groups of monkeys , although they were fed different diets and had different feeding times and access to food . The ages at which they dieted may also have come into play . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There is no compelling evidence caloric restriction will work with people , &amp;rdquo ; said Doug Gray , a molecular biologist with an interest in the role of protein homeostasis in aging and diseases of aging at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If this sounds like a depressing route to extreme longevity , even scientists agree . Noted one researcher : &amp;ldquo ; Life might seem longer , but it wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily be longer . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The intervention : &lt;/strong&gt; Gene editing &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;span class= " ILfuVd " &gt;&lt;span class= " e24Kjd " &gt;Genome editing , or gene editing , is a type of genetic engineering in which DNA is inserted , deleted , modified or **34;18843;TOOLONG . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last February , for example , the journal Nature Medicine reported on a therapy using &lt;span class= " ILfuVd " &gt;&lt;span class= " e24Kjd " &gt;CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology aimed at **26;18879;TOOLONG suppressing rapid aging in mice with the rare genetic disorder progeria , which causes accelerated aging . According to the report , two months after the therapy , the progeria mice were stronger and more active and had better heart health . Their lifespan also increased by about 25 per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The verdict so far : &lt;/strong&gt; Not ready for prime time , said Boling . Even though we have successfully mapped the human genome , and it&amp;rsquo ; s technically possible to remove a gene sequence and replace it , we have yet to successfully edit genes in a complex organism . Many people don&amp;rsquo ; t want to eat food containing genetically-modified organisms , let alone become one , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I don&amp;rsquo ; t think we have a clear handle on a special gene sequence that would essentially change the aging process . I would want to see if we could do it in a limited and focused way without undue downstream consequences . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;18907;TOOLONG ... title= " In 2017 , researchers at Stanford University medical school reported that injections of blood plasma from donors between the ages of 18 and 30 showed promise for helping human Alzheimer 's patients with mild to moderate symptoms regain some ability to perform basic daily tasks . " alt= " In 2017 , researchers at Stanford University medical school reported that injections of blood plasma from donors between the ages of 18 and 30 showed promise for helping human Alzheimer 's patients with mild to moderate symptoms regain some ability to perform basic daily tasks . " data-portal-copyright= " Colleen De Neve Colleen De Neve " **28;18943;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1546888 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The intervention : &lt;/strong&gt; Young blood &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; There have been a number of studies that looked at whether giving old mice blood from young mice could reverse some signs of aging . Even the researchers admitted it sounded creepy , but the results were intriguing . One study at the University of California , Berkeley , published in 2018 , found that &lt;span class= " jsx-671803276 " &gt;old mice showed benefits , including better muscle repair , from receiving blood from young mice . But young mice who received old blood had negative effects , including performing poorly on a strength test . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2017 , researchers at Stanford University medical school reported that injections of blood plasma from donors between the ages of 18 and 30 showed promise for helping human Alzheimer&amp;rsquo ; s patients with mild to moderate symptoms regain some ability to perform basic daily tasks , such as remembering to take their medications or preparing meals . The results were based on reports from the patients and their caregivers . The researchers cautioned that more research is needed , since the trial involved only nine patients who had received plasma infusions and nine who had received a placebo saline infusion. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;The verdict so far : &lt;/strong&gt; Don&amp;rsquo ; t try it . In a statement last February , the FDA said it had &amp;ldquo ; significant public health concerns&amp;rdquo ; about establishments that offer infusions of plasma from young donors to treat conditions ranging from normal aging and memory loss to Parkinson&amp;rsquo ; s disease , multiple sclerosis , Alzheimer&amp;rsquo ; s disease , and PTSD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Simply put , we&amp;rsquo ; re concerned that some patients are being preyed upon by unscrupulous actors touting treatments of plasma from young donors as cures and remedies . Such treatments have no proven clinical benefits for the uses for which these clinics are advertising them and are potentially harmful , &amp;rdquo ; warned the FDA. &amp;ldquo ; There are reports of bad actors charging thousands of dollars for infusions that are unproven and not guided by evidence from adequate and well-controlled trials . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;18973;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;19015;TOOLONG ... this rare disease could help treat aspects of **26;19050;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;19078;TOOLONG ... would you do with 20 extra years ? Scientists are close to extending a human 's ' healthy lifespan ' &lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt; &lt;/ul&gt; Joanne LauciusThu , 30 Jan 2020 13:17:45 **45;19113;TOOLONG ... shortages will continue without innovative solutions : drug policy experthttp : **34;19160;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;19196;TOOLONG ... title= " Jacalyn Duffin , Queen 's University in Kingston , ON " alt= " Jacalyn Duffin , Queen 's University in Kingston , ON " data-portal-copyright= " Lars Hagberg " **28;19232;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1516922 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Shortages of drugs that treat breast cancer and childhood leukemia have gotten much of the attention lately , but they represent just a small fraction of all the drug shortages in Canada right now . And such shortages will continue unless dramatic changes are made , says a Canadian drug policy expert . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jacalyn Duffin , professor emerita at Queens University who held the Hannah Chair for the History of Medicine until 2017 , said the federal government has to do a better job of measuring and understanding the cause and the scope of drug shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We can not talk about the drug shortage problem until we know what it is and how it changes over time . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2018 , Duffin and colleagues produced a report published by the C.D. Howe Institute that assessed Canada&amp;rsquo ; s drug shortage problem . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the time , they recommended Health Canada provide annual reports on drug shortages in an effort to &amp;ldquo ; define it , explain it and help provide solutions to mitigate the risks associated with the shortages . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The authors also recommended Health Canada measured the medical necessity of drugs to help prioritize solutions to shortages and that Canada encourage increased self-reliance in the manufacture of drugs and active ingredients in drugs &amp;mdash ; meaning produce its own . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In an interview , Duffin noted that Health Canada is still not measuring and analyzing drug shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In an update on tamoxifen shortages , Health Canada said it assesses the severity and potential impact of drug shortages when they occur . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Many shortages can be resolved through supply management measures without their effect ever being felt by patients . Health Canada works closely with the Canadian companies that supply drugs , the provinces and territories , and health stakeholders across the supply chain to identify and facilitate mitigation measures , as needed . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Along with a better understanding of the scope of ongoing shortages , she said , Canada should consider making its own generic drugs and drug ingredients as a buffer against some shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It blows me away that in a country like Canada with intellectual capital and human resources , we don&amp;rsquo ; t just start making them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;19262;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;19304;TOOLONG ... of reach : When cancer treatment is available but not **31;19339;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the U.S. , a group of hospitals and medical insurance groups formed a non-profit generic drug manufacturing company out of frustration over continuing shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has a mandatory drug shortage and discontinuation database , drugshortagescanada.ca , which is operated by Bell Canada under contract with Health Canada . According to the website , there are currently 1,966 drug shortages and 52 anticipated drug shortages in Canada . The site lists , but does not analyze the shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among drugs that continue to face shortages are tamoxifen , commonly prescribed for women with estrogen positive breast cancer . For weeks , patients have reported difficulty filling their prescriptions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Apotex , which is the country&amp;rsquo ; s biggest supplier of tamoxifen , expects to have supply available &amp;ldquo ; as soon as possible , &amp;rdquo ; said Jordan Burman , vice-president of global corporate communications . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The company had initially said the drug would be available by the end of January , but after working with Health Canada has since moved that up twice , said Burman . He said he expects the shortage to end before Dec. 31 , its current target . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said the shortage was due to a change in the manufacturing and formulation process . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We recognize the emotional burden it creates for patients and that is why we have accelerated the time line twice . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Vincristine , a chemotherapy used to treat childhood leukemia is also in short supply as are other cancer treatments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At CHEO , children have had to miss treatments because of the shortage of the leukemia drug . Shortages are expected to continue until at least the end of January . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a recent blog , Duffin said the reasons for drug shortages are complex and remain poorly understood . But she noted that numerous companies have stopped making some generic drugs , because the prices are so low . In 1996 , there were at least eight companies supplying tamoxifen in Canada . Now there are three . That has likely accelerated shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When there are only a few makers , the margin in the system is narrow . Any manufacturing problem will result in shortage , &amp;rdquo ; she wrote . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We as a society accept the notion that drug marketing and drug development belongs in the private sector . She went to the bathroom to get a glass of water , but when she pushed against the door , it wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t open . She thought that perhaps her daughter Melony&amp;rsquo ; s boyfriend , who often stayed over on weekends , was passed out on the floor , so she went back to bed for another hour before she had to get up to get ready for work . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Lorraine had only been in Ottawa for six weeks , after driving from Alberta and reconnecting with Melony , 42 , whom she&amp;rsquo ; d seen fewer than a handful of times since moving out west in 2000 . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;19765;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509019 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2008 , 14 people in Ottawa died as a result of unintentional opioid overdoses . In 2016 , the year that Melony died , there were 40. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last year , despite ongoing harm-reduction efforts aimed at preventing such deaths , that number ballooned to 82 , a nearly six-fold increase in the city&amp;rsquo ; s opioid mortality rate over the past decade , underlining the exploding emergency that communities , lawmakers , health-care professionals and families have so far been powerless to even contain , let alone eliminate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And make no mistake : this is a crisis . Last year alone , nearly 4,600 Canadians died of apparent opioid-related causes , or one person every hour and 55 minutes . The current mortality rate from opioids in this country is about twice that of HIV/AIDS at its peak in 1995 , while opioid overdoses take as many lives in Canada every four days as the number that died in this country as a result of the SARS epidemic . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Opioids have claimed more Canadian lives than any infectious epidemic since the Spanish flu that ravaged the world following the First World War , while in Ottawa , opioids are closing even that gap : if current trends continue , the death toll from opioid overdoses since 2005 in Ottawa &amp;mdash ; it stood at 444 heading into 2019 &amp;mdash ; will , before the end of this year , eclipse the roughly 520 Ottawans who perished from the flu . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2015-16 , meanwhile , more than nine million opioid prescriptions were filled in Ontario &amp;mdash ; two for every three residents . In Ottawa , the rate was only slightly lower , with 57 prescriptions for every 100 people . Nearly two million Ontarians &amp;mdash ; 14 per cent of the population &amp;mdash ; filled opioid prescriptions that year , while an estimated one in eight people taking opioids for chronic pain develops an addiction , or substance use disorder . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But like a distant radio station fading in and out during a long car ride , the general public&amp;rsquo ; s awareness of the growing catastrophe comes in fits and starts , typically brought into focus when two or three deaths among suburban youths , compressed into just a few days , are reported . Hands are wrung , thoughts and prayers offered , calls to action made , and then things return to normal . The trouble with normal in this case , however , is that it&amp;rsquo ; s worsening at an alarming rate . Frontline responders are unable to keep up , using , as Ottawa Inner City Health executive director Wendy Muckle describes it , &amp;ldquo ; a teacup to put out a house fire . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The bodies , &amp;rdquo ; she warns , &amp;ldquo ; are piling up . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And they&amp;rsquo ; re piling up everywhere . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h3&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;19795;TOOLONG ...
