But you never know . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The manner of Simon&amp;rsquo ; s death not only points to a growing trend in opioid use in Canada , but is also illustrative of some of the difficulties faced by health-care providers grappling with the issue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As Rob Boyd , director of the Oasis harm reduction program at the Sandy Hill Community Health Centre , points out , the homeless or at-risk population that accounts for roughly 10 per cent of accidental opioid deaths in Ontario was once the group hardest to pin down and treat . These days , they&amp;rsquo ; re the people most often taking part in harm reduction , such as attending supervised consumption sites . It&amp;rsquo ; s the construction workers who are self-medicating with illicit substances while alone in their basements , or the high school students using drugs of uncertain strengths , who often don&amp;rsquo ; t see themselves in this picture , he says , so precautions such as not consuming substances alone and having a naloxone kit handy &amp;mdash ; which can reverse the effects of an overdose &amp;mdash ; go unheeded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For many , too , a substance use disorder , or addiction , attaches itself to an unbearable weight of stigma and shame . &amp;ldquo ; The message is getting out to call 911 in all overdoses , even if it is reversed with naloxone , because the overdose can return when the naloxone wears off , &amp;rdquo ; says Matthew Young , a senior research and policy analyst at the Canadian Centre for Substance Use and Addiction ( CCSA ) . &amp;ldquo ; But there&amp;rsquo ; s a lot of reluctance to do that because it&amp;rsquo ; s a stigmatized , illegal activity , and a lot of people who are reticent to call 911 are those who have experienced an overdose in the suburban environment , because they don&amp;rsquo ; t want the police showing up at their house , even if it&amp;rsquo ; s a loved one who is there . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Peter and Kathie are speaking out about Simon&amp;rsquo ; s death because they feel that not talking about it only serves to reinforce the shame aspect of overdose fatalities . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re finally seeing people have open and honest discussions about the problem , &amp;rdquo ; says Peter . &amp;ldquo ; Would I have said this five or 10 years ago ? No , maybe I would have just hung my head in shame . But I&amp;rsquo ; m not ashamed of my son . I&amp;rsquo ; m sad , and it will never go away , but we don&amp;rsquo ; t shame people with cancer , we don&amp;rsquo ; t shame people with broken ribs . We&amp;rsquo ; re just getting around to not shaming people with mental illness . That&amp;rsquo ; s breaking the wall , and I think once that wall is a bit more broken down , we can get around to the substance use . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In Simon&amp;rsquo ; s case , &amp;rdquo ; he adds , &amp;ldquo ; he had anxiety and some depression , and so what do you do ? If you&amp;rsquo ; re not getting to the core of that , you&amp;rsquo ; re going to start self-medicating . Cocaine , alcohol , opioids , or a mix of all three . That&amp;rsquo ; s what people do . If you don&amp;rsquo ; t have good social and mental-health support , as well as realistic drug education , that&amp;rsquo ; s what will happen . Because of the shame and the lack of support , this is what people will do , and they will do it in the most dangerous way possible : late at night , in your basement , when no one&amp;rsquo ; s watching , when you&amp;rsquo ; ve had a couple of drinks . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;19991;TOOLONG ... title= " Simon Eady ( R ) with his sister , Samantha . Simon was 24 when he died of an opioid overdose in 2017. " alt= " Simon Eady ( R ) with his sister , Samantha . Simon was 24 when he died of an opioid overdose in 2017. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;20027;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509084 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Throw in a drug supply that includes counterfeit pills or other drugs laced with fentanyl , a synthetic opioid up to 100 times more potent than morphine , or carfentanil , a veterinary opioid 10,000 times as potent as morphine , and the results , as we&amp;rsquo ; ve seen , are disastrous . People are often overdosing on opioids while completely oblivious that they&amp;rsquo ; re even taking them , or believing they&amp;rsquo ; re consuming a prescription opioid &amp;mdash ; Percocet , for example &amp;mdash ; unaware that what they&amp;rsquo ; re taking is an illegally pressed pill possibly containing a lethal dose . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You don&amp;rsquo ; t know whether it&amp;rsquo ; s a street drug or a pharmaceutical drug or whatever , &amp;rdquo ; says Peter . &amp;ldquo ; You really don&amp;rsquo ; t know what&amp;rsquo ; s in there . The average person taking it isn&amp;rsquo ; t a pharmacist , isn&amp;rsquo ; t a chemist , and doesn&amp;rsquo ; t understand what might happen . And somebody might be able to wake up the next morning and feel a bit dazed , and other people might not wake up . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , people with substance use disorders who don&amp;rsquo ; t die from their overdoses are increasingly turning up at hospital emergency departments . In 2018 , Ottawa-area hospitals reported 471 emergency department visits for opioid overdoses , a 27 per cent increase over the 370 a year earlier , and almost twice the 243 seen in 2016. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Current measures in place , including supervised consumption sites ( Ottawa has four : Ottawa Inner City Health&amp;rsquo ; s trailer at the Shepherds of Good Hope on Murray Street ; the Sandy Hill Community Health Centre , on Nelson Street ; Somerset West Community Health Centre , on Eccles Street ; and Ottawa Public Health&amp;rsquo ; s , on Clarence Street ) ; legislated changes to Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s pharmaceutical drug supply ; widespread access to naloxone ; and agonist treatment &amp;mdash ; replacing such drugs as heroin and fentanyl with safer , longer-lasting opioids such as methadone or suboxone , to ease withdrawal symptoms &amp;mdash ; are only serving to slow the invasive tide , not reverse it , as the number of deaths continues to rise each year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20057;TOOLONG ... title= " Rob Boyd , Director of Oasis Program poses for a photo at the Sandy Hill Community Health Centre in Ottawa Thursday April 25 , 2019 . The health centre wanted to show how they use a mass spectrometer to determine whether or not a product has any carfentanyl. " alt= " Rob Boyd , Director of Oasis Program poses for a photo at the Sandy Hill Community Health Centre in Ottawa Thursday April 25 , 2019 . The health centre wanted to show how they use a mass spectrometer to determine whether or not a product has any carfentanyl. " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;20093;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509077 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; At Sandy Hill&amp;rsquo ; s supervised consumption site , people who use substances can test them to find out what they contain . It&amp;rsquo ; s the only such program in Ottawa , while Vancouver is the only other Canadian city currently offering the service . At Sandy Hill , they&amp;rsquo ; ve discovered fentanyl in everything : heroin , cocaine , crack , even cannabis . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We see swings of the different drugs on a regular basis , &amp;rdquo ; says Ottawa Inner City Health medical director Dr. Jeffrey Turnbull . &amp;ldquo ; We always have fentanyl now . The one thing that is not in the heroin &amp;hellip ; is heroin . It&amp;rsquo ; s almost all fentanyl or carfentanil or some other drug &amp;ndash ; benzodiazepines , methadone &amp;mdash ; mixed in with it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are newer metabolites available all the time , &amp;rdquo ; he adds . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s small amounts , easy to traffic , can be synthesized relatively easily , and very addictive and very potent . And it&amp;rsquo ; s very hard to detect . And you&amp;rsquo ; ve got a ready market for it . Wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t this be your dream if you were in the drug trade ? So I think we&amp;rsquo ; re going to have a lot of trouble arresting our way out of this problem . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to Statistics Canada , the opioid crisis is the main factor behind its findings earlier this year that the life expectancy of Canadians at birth failed to increase from 2016 to 2017 , as deaths due to opioids wiped out health gains made by improved treatments for cancer and heart disease . It marked the first time in four decades that Canadians&amp;rsquo ; average life expectancy stalled . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; How did we get here ? Both Boyd and Turnbull refer to the &amp;ldquo ; perfect storm&amp;rdquo ; of events that laid this mess at our feet , beginning in the 1980s when palliative care and pain management became a hot-button issue in Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Turnbull , who was then a practising physician , says that pain was not being adequately addressed at the time , and many among the palliative-care movement were arguing that , like blood pressure , pulse and respiration , it should be treated as a vital sign . Some physicians , however , voiced their concerns about patients possibly becoming addicted to painkillers. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Then along came the Purdue Pharma&amp;rsquo ; s 1996 release of OxyContin , a powerful oxycodone painkiller that was added to Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s drug formulary &amp;mdash ; meaning doctors here could prescribe it &amp;mdash ; in 2000 . The drug was effective and , Purdue promised , not addictive . &amp;ldquo ; And we just jumped on it , &amp;rdquo ; recalls Turnbull . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20123;TOOLONG ... title= " FILE PHOTO : Bottles of prescription painkiller OxyContin , 40mg pills , made by Purdue Pharma L.D. sit on a shelf at a local pharmacy , in Provo , Utah , U.S. , April 25 , 2017. " alt= " FILE PHOTO : Bottles of prescription painkiller OxyContin , 40mg pills , made by Purdue Pharma L.D. sit on a shelf at a local pharmacy , in Provo , Utah , U.S. , April 25 , 2017. " data-portal-copyright= " George Frey " **28;20159;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509082 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; As it turned out , though , the drug was highly addictive . Many people were bypassing its slow-release formulation by crushing the pills and snorting the powder , or mixing it with water and injecting it . Street users , says Turnbull , called it hillbilly heroin . &amp;ldquo ; It was being widely used . But those messages were not being heard . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; And then ( Purdue ) lost their patent protection . You would think that there was an opportunity to say , &amp;lsquo ; No , we&amp;rsquo ; re not going to open this up to the world , &amp;rsquo ; but instead , we opened it up to the world , and prescriptions went up . &amp;rdquo ; In 2010 , meanwhile , as a way of extending its hold on the market , Purdue , citing greater safety precautions , released a new formulation for OxyContin , called OxyNEO , that was more difficult to crush or inject . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As Oxy&amp;rsquo ; s addictive properties had become more evident , doctors were increasingly reluctant to prescribe it , and in 2012 , OxyContin was delisted from Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s formularly . OxyNEO was added , but its availability was more restricted . This , says Turnbull , completed the first phase of the perfect storm : create a substance addiction epidemic &amp;mdash ; an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 Ontarians had by then become addicted to opioids , he says &amp;mdash ; and then remove the substance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The second phase of the storm was the illicit drug trade that filled the newly created vacuum . &amp;ldquo ; We didn&amp;rsquo ; t have treatment facilities or counselling , &amp;rdquo ; says Turnbull , &amp;ldquo ; and who was there waiting for that group of people but the people who produce heroin ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Suddenly , the banged-up thirtysome-year-old construction worker &amp;mdash ; the industry identified as perhaps the hardest-hit by the opioid crisis , accounting for about 30 per cent of accidental fatalities in Ontario last year where the deceased&amp;rsquo ; s occupation was known &amp;mdash ; was associating with criminal elements to address their pain , and by and large using the substance alone in their home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Then came the fentanyl wave . The drug , up to 100 times more potent than morphine , had been around in patch form , typically used by cancer patients , since the 1990s . But it wasn&amp;rsquo ; t until the 2012 delisting of OxyContin that it found greater widespread use . By 2015 or &amp;rsquo ; 16 , says Turnbull , it had become a recreational drug . Health-care and enforcement officials in Ottawa helplessly watched as it spread west , from B.C. to Alberta and , eventually , Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We knew it was going to be Phase 3 , &amp;rdquo ; says Turnbull . &amp;ldquo ; We had all these people on heroin and we had a highly addictive new drug coming , and it was easy to synthesize and easy to transport . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It just happened overnight , and it devastated the community . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20189;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Jeff Turnbull of Ottawa Inner City Health . " alt= " Dr. Jeff Turnbull of Ottawa Inner City Health . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;20225;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509066 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to Boyd , the switch from largely stolen or otherwise diverted fentanyl patches to illicitly manufactured powdered fentanyl was a tipping point . &amp;ldquo ; Nobody saw it coming , and it was such a game-changer . It changed all the rules to how we were approaching this problem and how we were going to solve it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Fentanyl was going to create challenges in and of itself , &amp;rdquo ; he adds , &amp;ldquo ; but once we got to the illicit fentanyl , we really lost control . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Globalization , advances in information technology and the dark web also combined to make matters worse , says Matthew Young from the CCSA . Many of the illicit synthetic opioids that came on the market were based on analgesics that had been tested by pharmaceutical companies but never commercially developed . It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t that difficult for a trafficker to Google an old patent and send the specifications to a chemical manufacturer in China to have it produced . The dealer would then mix the chemical with powder , stamp it out as pills , and start selling it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Young notes that the Drug Enforcement Agency in the U.S. and the RCMP here in Canada have done a lot of work with their colleagues in China to curb this practice . Five or six years ago when it was more prevalent , part of the attraction to dealers was that the drugs had never actually been on the pharmaceutical market before , and because they weren&amp;rsquo ; t specifically referred to in Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Controlled Drugs and Substances Act , they technically weren&amp;rsquo ; t illegal . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But there&amp;rsquo ; s a saying in toxicology that the dose makes the poison , &amp;rdquo ; says Young , &amp;ldquo ; and the challenge with a potent chemical like fentanyl and carfentanil is that these clandestine labs had a very challenging time getting an even distribution of the substance throughout the product that they were going to sell . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In other words , while one pill or injection might get you to that sweet spot you&amp;rsquo ; d been chasing , the next one you take an hour later could well kill you . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So while it was bad enough to have thousands and thousands of people addicted to opioids , the crisis became exponentially worse when increasing numbers of them started showing up in morgues . And as long as illicit fentanyl and more toxic analogues such as carfentanil are contaminating the street drug supply , the problem , says Boyd , isn&amp;rsquo ; t going to improve . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Fundamentally , we really have to address this toxic supply of drugs that is out there . We have to go back to the problem we had in 2012 , which was the problem with OxyContin . We need to go back to a point where there was at least some level of control . Fentanyl has really challenged all the tools that we have to fight this . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Adding to the perfect storm described by Turnbull , Boyd points to other factors that exacerbated the opioid crisis &amp;mdash ; an aging population that feels entitled to live pain-free ; a strained primary health-care system focused on the flow-through of patients , making the prescription of drugs preferred over other , longer-term , treatments ; and a shift to a knowledge-based economy that pushed great swaths of the labour force to under- or unemployment , as jobs moved offshore to Third World countries . It&amp;rsquo ; s no coincidence that the opioid crisis is particularly bad in what are considered rust-belt communities , where auto plants have shuttered and other manufacturing industries closed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20255;TOOLONG ... title= " A Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) chemist checks confiscated powder containing fentanyl at the DEA Northeast Regional Laboratory on October 8 , 2019 in New York . " alt= " A Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) chemist checks confiscated powder containing fentanyl at the DEA Northeast Regional Laboratory on October 8 , 2019 in New York . " data-portal-copyright= " DON EMMERT " **28;20291;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509071 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Think of London , Ontario when ( General Motors ) was pulling out of there , and Oshawa now , &amp;rdquo ; says Boyd . In the U.S. , it&amp;rsquo ; s West Virginia , Ohio , Pennsylvania and Kentucky that are hurting the most . &amp;ldquo ; Those are the areas of highest prescribing of opioids because people didn&amp;rsquo ; t have anything to do , &amp;rdquo ; says Boyd . &amp;ldquo ; You can put up with a lot of pain if you&amp;rsquo ; ve got a job to get up and go to and if you have responsibilities . But you take that away and the depression and pain come in &amp;mdash ; mood disorders and depression can manifest as pain in your body . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; So people are feeling unwell and unhappy . They&amp;rsquo ; re depressed and are legitimately feeling aches and pains . So you&amp;rsquo ; ve got downturns in the economy and social disruption happens from that . There&amp;rsquo ; s a growing sense of disconnect . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That growing sense of disconnect is a major theme in journalist/researcher Johann Hari&amp;rsquo ; s book Chasing the Scream : The First and Last Days of the War on Drugs . &amp;ldquo ; The opposite of addiction isn&amp;rsquo ; t sobriety , &amp;rdquo ; he insists , &amp;ldquo ; it&amp;rsquo ; s connection . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s position as a white-collar , government and hi-tech city has given it some insulation from the towering mortality rates that have plagued many other Ontario municipalities. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The city&amp;rsquo ; s 82 accidental opioid-related deaths last year put its rate at 8.1 deaths for every 100,000 residents , slightly less than the provincial average of 10.2 and well below Thunder Bay&amp;rsquo ; s 28.5 , the highest in Ontario . ( Were Ottawa to match Thunder Bay&amp;rsquo ; s rate , the death toll last year would have been 288 , or 11 people every two weeks . ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other cities or regions with extremely high mortality rates last year included Hamilton ( 21.3 per 100,000 ) , Niagara ( 19.2 ) , Peterborough ( 18.8 ) , Haliburton ( 16.2 ) and Sudbury ( 16.0 ) . Toronto&amp;rsquo ; s 2018 rate of 10 people per 100,000 was just under the provincial average , while London , Windsor , Kingston , North Bay and Kitchener/Waterloo were all slightly higher . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are a lot of protective factors for people around substance use and substance use disorder , &amp;rdquo ; says Boyd . &amp;ldquo ; Education , stable housing , basic economic stability , and that other piece around social connections . And a lot of that comes through employment , so if you&amp;rsquo ; ve got good employment , you&amp;rsquo ; re probably OK . So Ottawa is a bit of a bubble , with the public service . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20321;TOOLONG ... title= " Wendy Muckle of Ottawa Inner City Health . " alt= " Wendy Muckle of Ottawa Inner City Health . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;20357;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509068 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa , says Muckle , somewhat benefits from its size : it&amp;rsquo ; s large enough of a city that it has numerous agencies and services that might not be available to residents of smaller communities , while at the same time not being so large as to have to duplicate services . &amp;ldquo ; Ottawa tends to be able to have a more coordinated approach , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; Everyone tends to do things together , whereas in Toronto there tends to be a group working on this and another group working on that , because it&amp;rsquo ; s so big . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s opioid mortality is nonetheless exploding , in both number and rate , as well as against the provincial average : In 2012 , Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s opioid-related mortality rate was 2.1 per 100,000 , less than half of the province&amp;rsquo ; s 4.4 that year . Last year&amp;rsquo ; s rate of 8.1 &amp;mdash ; nearly quadruple the 2012 rate &amp;mdash ; was about 80 per cent of the Ontario rate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other indicators add to a less-than-rosy picture here : the 444 opioid-related visits to emergency rooms in Ottawa last year was 20 per cent more than in 2017 , and an increase of nearly 150 per cent from the 178 trips in 2015. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many at the front lines believe that the opioid crisis has to be treated as a health crisis , and not a criminal one . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If this was something else , like cancer , we&amp;rsquo ; d be taking it far more seriously , &amp;rdquo ; says Peter Eady . &amp;ldquo ; But because there&amp;rsquo ; s that base level of puritanism in our society , we treat it like , &amp;lsquo ; Just say no , &amp;rsquo ; and we know that&amp;rsquo ; s not effective . The prohibition model hasn&amp;rsquo ; t worked . The war on drugs was lost years ago , and all it&amp;rsquo ; s done is destroy countries like Bolivia , Columbia , Mexico and the , let&amp;rsquo ; s call them the consumer societies &amp;mdash ; U.S. , Western Europe and whatnot. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He cites Portugal and Switzerland as examples of countries where progressive policies , including decriminalization and substitution therapy , have had considerable success easing the problem . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He additionally praises such initiatives as Project Step , an Ottawa-based organization that provides support , treatment , education and prevention of youth addictions , as well as the Community Addictions Peer Support Association and The Canadian Drug Policy Coalition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But we could do a lot better , &amp;rdquo ; he says , &amp;ldquo ; and the present methods ( of criminalization and incarceration ) aren&amp;rsquo ; t working . Even most thoughtful law-enforcement officials know that . If we had a safe supply and better integrated it with the health system , I think you&amp;rsquo ; d get a much better result . The stats around the world seem to suggest it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; At least it&amp;rsquo ; s now being discussed openly , &amp;rdquo ; he says , &amp;ldquo ; and maybe things will change . I can only hope so . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20387;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Vera Etches , head of Ottawa Public Health , in Ottawa Friday Oct 25 , 2019. " alt= " Dr. Vera Etches , head of Ottawa Public Health , in Ottawa Friday Oct 25 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;20423;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509067 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Vera Etches , Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s chief medical officer of health , notes that there are about 40,000 people in Ottawa who have said they used illicit substances in the last year . &amp;ldquo ; Not everyone is in trouble with that use ; there&amp;rsquo ; s a spectrum of use . Some people find beneficial aspects &amp;mdash ; they&amp;rsquo ; re stable and able to manage their lives and their families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But when someone starts to have a disorder , that&amp;rsquo ; s a crisis for each of those families . When you see 82 deaths and you see the deaths rising , that&amp;rsquo ; s distressing . And each of those families and many more are in crisis . So to me , the label you put on it is not as important as the action we&amp;rsquo ; re taking to address it . What&amp;rsquo ; s important is , are we moving ahead urgently ? Because people are in distress and things are going the wrong way still . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At its budget presentation to the Ottawa Board of Health earlier this month , Ottawa Public Health recommended the adoption of the Ottawa Community Action Plan , a mental health and substance use strategy focusing on opioid use . The plan proposes collaborative efforts by OPH , the CCSA , The Royal , the Community Addictions Peer Support Association and other stakeholders to address stigma and language issues related to substance use and mental health ; an increase in harm reduction initiatives and access to them ; and integrating access to comprehensive mental health , substance use and social services . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That said , Ottawa Public Health also had to find $1.4 million in &amp;ldquo ; efficiencies&amp;rdquo ; in its 2020 budget . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Can the crisis deepen ? &amp;ldquo ; Yes , &amp;rdquo ; says Turnbull , &amp;ldquo ; it can get a whole lot worse , with new derivatives that are more toxic , or if it gets out and spreads beyond the traditional drug-using population and gets in high schools and other areas where it becomes more recreational . Absolutely it can get worse . At the moment , we&amp;rsquo ; re struggling to keep up and to keep people alive . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Etches agrees , and wonders , too , how social determinants could further come into play . &amp;ldquo ; What if unemployment increases ? What if the rates of poverty increase ? Those to me would be big drivers of stress , and then of potential substance use , and then problematic substance use . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We want to be building a society where there are supports when people need them to keep them out of dire situations . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other agencies are engaging the crisis . The Ottawa chapter of Bereaved Families of Ontario , for example , which offers peer support groups at the Bronson Centre for people grieving the loss of a family member or friend , this month started a group dedicated to those who have lost someone to substance use . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20453;TOOLONG ... title= " Lorraine Lefebvre daughter , Melony as a youngster . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;20489;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509079 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Lorraine Lefebvre , who was in therapy following her daughter Melony&amp;rsquo ; s death , had heard two years ago of Bereaved Families&amp;rsquo ; 10-week support group for those who had lost a child , so she joined . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It helped me immensely , to deal with a lot of the anger , the guilt , the shame and grief , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; It doesn&amp;rsquo ; t go away , but I&amp;rsquo ; ve learned to live with it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This past May , Lorraine started volunteering in BFO&amp;rsquo ; s office , keeping records , setting up chairs for meetings , getting the coffee and cookies ready , greeting people at meetings and signing them in. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I found my purpose , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; It gave me joy to come in here every day . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; More recently , Lorraine completed the facilitators&amp;rsquo ; course , and is now leading the loss-of-child group . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She says that since she began volunteering there six months ago , 56 new clients have come to the centre , each having lost someone to substance use . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Why is no one paying attention ? &amp;rdquo ; she asks . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **30;20519;TOOLONG " **37;20551;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;20590;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " http : **34;20632;TOOLONG ... they buy those drugs , it 's a loaded gun ' &lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;20668;TOOLONG ... no blood test for addiction ' : Troubling data in the opioid **27;20703;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;20732;TOOLONG ... shame of opioids : Confronting the crisis by addressing **27;20767;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;20796;TOOLONG ... " alt= " A 2016 file photo of Dr. Joel Lexchin. " data-portal-copyright= " Tyler Anderson/Naitonal Post " **28;20984;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1509861 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ontario government is proposing drug regulation changes that it says will remove red tape and barriers for pharmaceutical companies , allowing some drugs to bypass the normal approval process during a shortage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21014;TOOLONG ... shortages , including the often-used breast cancer drug tamoxifen&lt;/a&gt; , have been wide-spread and increasing in recent years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The move , the government says , would allow alternative drug products to quickly enter the market during a shortage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; However , the move is being met with resistance by some drug policy experts who say more information is needed to ensure the changes are good for consumers &amp;mdash ; and whether the changes will actually help prevent long-term drug shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The changes , part of the government&amp;rsquo ; s larger push to reduce red tape , would also make it easier for companies to raise or lower drug prices in other cases , depending on the market . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a document about the proposed changes , the government says they would ensure that Ontario remains &amp;ldquo ; open for business&amp;rdquo ; for the pharmacy and pharmaceutical industry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The proposals , called &amp;ldquo ; Reducing Administrative Burden to Drug Manufacturers and Pharmacies , &amp;rdquo ; are part of an omnibus red tape reduction bill that was introduced at the end of October while the legislature was recessed . They affect prescription drugs , mainly generics. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some drug policy experts fear the changes would remove some consumer protections , are being introduced with little publicity and will do little to address long-term drug shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Pharmaceutical policy expert Dr. Joel Lexchin , who teaches at York University&amp;rsquo ; s School of Health Policy and Management , said he is concerned about the lack of consultation and transparency around the changes . Some of the proposals respond to requests from the pharmaceutical industry with apparently little or no input from consumers or healthcare providers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; More details are needed , he said , before the changes go ahead . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It should not be the job of the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to advocate on behalf of the pharmaceutical industry . The job of the Ministry of Health should be the protection of the health of Ontarians , &amp;rdquo ; wrote Lexchin in a submission to the Ministry of Health . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Before the ministry goes ahead with these changes it needs to provide much more information and show that these changes will put the health of the people of Ontario above the interests of the commercial entities that are advocating for them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jacalyn Duffin , professor emerita and Hannah Chair of the History of Medicine at Queen&amp;rsquo ; s University , said she only learned about the proposals when a law firm blogged about them . She said she finds some of them shocking . &amp;ldquo ; They will remove some consumer protections and probably will not help the shortages . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The proposed changes include an amendment that would make it easier for generic drug companies to adjust their prices if the number of competitors on the market changes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Under the current model , generic drugs are priced at a percentage of the brand price , depending on how many competitors there are . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For example , if a brand label drug costs $10 , generic makers could charge $7.50 or $8 , but that price would decrease based on the number of competitors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The proposed changes allow drug companies to more easily adjust their prices when competitors come in and out of the market , something the government says should reduce the price of generic drugs . However , it could also allow companies to increase the price of generics , especially at a time of consolidations of drug companies and shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Justin Bates , Chief Executive Officer of the Ontario Pharmacists Association , said the change enables Ontario pharmacies to operate on a level playing field with pharmacies in every other province , except Quebec . Ordinary commercial terms are a normal part of business , he said , and do not increase drug costs , which are regulated by a Canada-wide system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The proposed changes would also exempt certain drugs from drug submission requirements , allowing quicker funding of a drug that could fill in during a shortage . Funding of the alternative drug would be temporary , the government says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A spokesman for Health Minister Christine Elliott dismissed concerns that the changes had been brought in quietly and with too little information , saying they were part of a &amp;ldquo ; high-profile&amp;rdquo ; government wide announcement of red tape reduction proposals and will help the government respond to patient needs in the event of potential drug shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The proposed changes would allow an alternative drug product to be temporarily funded under the Ontario Drug Benefit program during a supply interruption that may be due to a drug shortage &amp;hellip ; and is expected to lead to significant patient risk or harm , &amp;rdquo ; said Hayley Chazan , a spokesperson for Health Minister Christine Elliott . &amp;ldquo ; This proposal , if approved , would mitigate supply gaps of funded products for recipients of the Ontario Drug Benefit program . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But Lexchin said the proposed changes are simply reactive and lack any proactive measures to deal with future drug shortages . New Zealand , for example , requires drug companies to guarantee there will be sufficient supply before approving the drug for the health system . If the company runs out of drugs , it is then their responsibility to source a replacement , not the government&amp;rsquo ; s. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Paul Grootendorst , associate professor in the Faculty of Pharmacy at the University of Toronto said the proposed changes allowing generic companies to change their prices up or down when the number of competitors changes make sense . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I don&amp;rsquo ; t see any problems , &amp;rdquo ; he said of the proposals . &amp;ldquo ; These are more housekeeping issues . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The government is seeking comment on the proposals until Nov. 27. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; epayne@postmedia.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21049;TOOLONG ... bodies are piling up ' : Inside the opioid epidemic and the crisis that wo n't go away&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21084;TOOLONG ... concerned they ca n't provide proper care in crowded hospitals , says union&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21119;TOOLONG ... was bawling ' : Injured Bronco 's mother stunned by his progress after surgery&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneFri , 22 Nov 2019 11:39:55 **45;21154;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal NewsSeniorsWomenU.S. stem cell clinic offering unapproved therapies brings direct-to-consumer marketing to Ottawahttp : **34;21201;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;21237;TOOLONG ... title= " A doctor a private U.S. clinic injects a patient with stem cells to treat cartilage wastage joint injury and pain . " alt= " A doctor a private U.S. clinic injects a patient with stem cells to treat cartilage wastage joint injury and pain . " data-portal-copyright= " edward olive " **28;21273;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1507409 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Just a few months after Health Canada began cracking down on private clinics offering unapproved stem cell therapies , at least one U.S. clinic has moved in to fill the vacuum with direct marketing to Canadian consumers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The clinic from Burlington , Vermont , even offers shuttle buses to transport people from Ottawa to the clinic four hours away for treatment it suggests will end joint pain , among other things . Lunch and dinner are free , but each injection costs $6,880 . Two for $10,880. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The treatments , using umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells , are not approved in either Canada or the United States . Health Canada warns that Canadians who travel abroad for stem cell treatments &amp;ldquo ; may put themselves at risk . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While stem cells , which were discovered at the University of Toronto in 1961 by James Till and Ernest McCulloch , promise to revolutionize many treatments and could offer breakthroughs for diseases , almost all are still considered experimental and have yet to be proven safe or effective . Clinical trials on numerous potential stem cell therapies are under way , including in Ottawa . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While research progresses , private stem cell clinics have popped up around the world making promises for treatments not yet proven safe or effective . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A 2018 study by Leigh Turner of the University of Minnesota Center for Bioethics found 43 clinics offering stem cell treatments in Canada and 750 in the U.S. Earlier this year , Health Canada sent Canadian clinics , including some in Ottawa , cease-and-desist letters . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Clinics in Vermont , near the Canadian border , appear to have ramped up marketing to Canadians since then . One clinic has been holding back-to-back seminars . Another says it stopped marketing in Canada after receiving a warning from Health Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There have been cases of harm as a result of treatments , including two women who had permanent damage to their sight after stem cells were injected into their eyes at a Florida clinic . Other patients have been infected with unsterilized equipment and others have developed tumours at the site of stem cell injections. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A common harm , critics say , is exploitation . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;21303;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Michael Rudnicki is director of the regenerative medicine program and Sprott Centre for Stem Cell Research at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute , says of stem cell therapy claims : ' If it sounds too good to be true , it probably is too good to be true . ' " alt= " Dr. Michael Rudnicki is director of the regenerative medicine program and Sprott Centre for Stem Cell Research at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute , says of stem cell therapy claims : ' If it sounds too good to be true , it probably is too good to be true . ' " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;21339;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1507406 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health officials say the clinics are misusing the promise of stem cell therapy to exploit vulnerable patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These patients are in pain and they are suffering and they are looking for help and they are being exploited , &amp;rdquo ; said Dr. Michael Rudnicki , director of the regenerative medicine program and Sprott Centre for Stem Cell Research at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If it sounds too good to be true , it probably is too good to be true . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At a recent seminar at a west-end Ottawa hotel meeting room , Roseanna Ammendolea of the Vermont Center for Regenerative Medicine told a packed room that her clinic and others like it had successfully treated people for pain related to arthritis , neuropathy and other ailments that affected joints using mesenchymal stem cells from umbilical cords . The stem cells , she claimed , are both effective and safe , saying there had been no issues with cell rejection . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We will not give injections if we feel that this injection will not be beneficial to our patients . This is why we are so successful . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Participants , including some who walked with canes and others who talked about being in pain and having mobility issues , were shown videos of people described as Canadian clients who claimed the treatments worked . One man said it was &amp;ldquo ; probably the best money I have spent in my life as far as my health . &amp;rdquo ; Another said she would do it again &amp;ldquo ; in a heartbeat&amp;rdquo ; and was able to do things she hadn&amp;rsquo ; t been able to do earlier . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They were also shown a slide showing long wait times for hip and knee replacements in Ontario , &amp;ldquo ; We are not a priority , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &amp;ldquo ; Where does that leave us ? &amp;rdquo ; Participants weren&amp;rsquo ; t told exactly how the stem cells were supposed to work , but claimed they had successfully improved pain and mobility issues in clients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What the seminar goers weren&amp;rsquo ; t told is that , even in the U.S. , the treatment is not covered by health insurance because it remains unproven. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The U.S. Federal Drug Administration has issued a warning to consumers not to use cell therapies that are unapproved or unproven. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Stem cells have been called everything from cure-alls to miracle treatments . But don&amp;rsquo ; t believe the hype . Some unscrupulous providers offer stem cell products that are both unapproved and unproven . So beware of potentially dangerous procedures &amp;mdash ; and confirm what&amp;rsquo ; s really being offered before you consider &lt;em&gt;any&lt;/em&gt; &amp;nbsp ; treatment , &amp;rdquo ; the FDA said in a statement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The only stem-cell-based products that are FDA-approved for use in the United States are blood-forming stem cells derived from cord blood&amp;nbsp ; for limited use in patients with disorders affecting the body system that is involved in the production of blood . Bone marrow is also used for these treatments , but is generally not regulated by the FDA for that use . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health Canada has granted market authorization for a stem cell therapy to treat graft-versus-host disease and two cell-based gene therapies to treat certain cancers . Most cell therapies are still experimental . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I totally understand the skepticism of it , &amp;rdquo ; Doug Argento , who works at the Vermont Center for Regenerative Medicine , said in a telephone interview , &amp;ldquo ; but the fact is that things that are approved now and medically paid for were seen as renegade 20 or 30 years ago . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The treatment employs technology developed by Neil Riordan , founder , chairman and chief science officer of the Stem Cell Institute in Panama , using human umbilical cord tissue-derived mesenchymal stem cells . There are 41 such clinics across the U.S. Riordan also played a role in the development of a nutritional product called Stem-Kine , which producers claim &amp;mdash ; without scientific backing &amp;mdash ; increases the number of stem cells circulating in a person&amp;rsquo ; s body . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The stem cells injected in the clinic , Argento said , are from umbilical cord tissue as a result of caesarean births to reduce risk of infection . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rudnicki , of The Ottawa Hospital Research Institute , says there is &amp;ldquo ; no evidence that these sorts of cells are regenerative at all . It would not pass muster in Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The public has to understand that there are people out to remove them from their money . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rudnicki says he regularly receives inquiries from people desperate to get stem cell treatments . He says he tries to connect them with clinical trials that they might be able to participate in. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rudnicki noted there were multiple clinical trials in Canada , including treatments of autoimmune diseases , trials involving treatment for Type 1 diabetes and others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; But the use of these inappropriate cell types for treating arthritis and joints and so on is certainly not approved by Health Canada and would not be allowed in Canada under the regulations . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is some evidence that injections of some stem cell products might have a temporary positive impact on inflammation , he said , but it will not be regenerative and will not restore function to joints . &amp;ldquo ; They are being sold a bill of goods . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leigh Turner of the University of Minnesota Center for Bioethics , meanwhile , says the explosion in clinics offering unproven stem cell therapies in the U.S. is &amp;ldquo ; a marketplace that traffics in misrepresentation . It is easy to see how people are taken advantage of and scammed. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is also difficult to find out about physical harms being done to patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are no safety studies . We don&amp;rsquo ; t have good data . But we do know there have been some serious harms. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Stem cell therapies have the potential to become standard treatment in some areas , but they are not there yet , Turner said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Businesses are tapping into genuine human suffering , desperation and also hope . &amp;ldquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Turner also noted there was an &amp;ldquo ; excellent chance&amp;rdquo ; that the vials of liquid being injected into patients did not actually contain stem cells . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Jonathan Fenton of another stem cell clinic in Burlington , the Vermont Regenerative Medicine , said he had complained about the new clinic , the Vermont Center for Regenerative Medicine , which has a similar name and employs hard-sell tactics , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His clinic takes bone marrow from patients&amp;rsquo ; hips and injects it . The procedure is done the same day . He says he regularly sees Canadian patients for bone marrow aspiration therapy and platelet-rich plasma treatments , using their own blood . The treatments , he says , speed healing and are allowed in the U.S. The use of bone marrow aspiration is neither proven nor allowed in Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fenton , who is secretary-treasurer of the American Academy of Orthopedic Medicine , acknowledged many people offering stem cell treatments are &amp;ldquo ; not doing it to the highest ethical standards . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He has filed complaints with state officials over clinics selling unsafe or fraudulent treatments . &amp;ldquo ; I have asked the state and federal judiciary to close down this clinic for committing fraud . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said his platelet and bone marrow treatments were covered by a major Vermont health insurer because they saw the cost of benefits were going down and patients were requiring fewer surgeries . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said he was told by Health Canada that he could not market in Canada . Representatives of the Vermont Center for Regenerative Medicine , meanwhile , said they had discussions with Health Canada about what they could and could not say when marketing in Canada before holding seminars in Ottawa and Halifax . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have looked at the information provided and have not identified any immediate non-compliance with advertising regulations pertaining to Canadian health products , &amp;rdquo ; a Health Canada spokesperson said , adding that the agency was continuing to assess . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Back at a west-end Ottawa hotel , some participants in the seminar , including a retired pharmacist , said they were considering getting the treatments . &amp;ldquo ; But it&amp;rsquo ; s expensive . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another participant said he was skeptical. &amp;ldquo ; They seemed very sketchy when I went online . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;21369;TOOLONG " **34;21398;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21434;TOOLONG ... and Kaushic : We 're losing the fight against superbugs&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21469;TOOLONG ... who live to at least 110 , boast stronger immune systems , helping them fight off diseases&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21504;TOOLONG ... stimulator ' really promising ' : Survivor moves legs for first time since Humboldt bus crash&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneMon , 18 Nov 2019 11:51:22 **45;21539;TOOLONG ... **37;21586;TOOLONG upsetting ' : Breast cancer patients dealing with shortage of common drug treatmenthttp : **31;21625;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;21658;TOOLONG ... title= " Tricia Smith poses for a photo in Ottawa Monday Nov 11 , 2019 . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;21694;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1503625 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Tricia Smith tried to fill her prescription for tamoxifen two weeks ago , she was shocked by what she heard : The drug commonly prescribed for breast cancer patients is in short supply in Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Smith , who lives in Kanata , was told by the pharmacy she normally uses that the drug was on back order and not available : They couldn&amp;rsquo ; t fill her prescription . She tried another pharmacy only to be told that they had just eight tablets left ( she usually gets 100 at a time ) . Finally , she found a local drug store that was able to fill her entire prescription . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She was lucky . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is a shortage of tamoxifen across the country and it could last until the end of January , say officials . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Smith said she wasn&amp;rsquo ; t too concerned when she was originally told that the drug was on back order since her supply wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t run out for a few weeks . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Then I got more concerned , not only for myself but for other women , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For thousands of Ontario patients who have been prescribed the drug to reduce the chance of breast cancer recurring , such a shortage is terrifying . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We take this very seriously , because we know this is very upsetting for patients , &amp;rdquo ; said Dr. Leta Forbes , a medical oncologist and provincial head of Cancer Care Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s systemic treatment program . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cancer Care Ontario , the Ontario government agency tasked with improving cancer care , and health-care professionals &amp;ldquo ; understand that this is incredibly upsetting for patients and our No. 1 priority is to make sure the patient is supported when we are going through a drug shortage and to give them the information they need , &amp;rdquo ; said Forbes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There have been increasing drug shortages across the country in recent years &amp;mdash ; for a complex variety of reasons . Those shortages have included cancer drugs , including some commonly used for children . At CHEO in Ottawa , two children who needed a drug for acute lymphoblastic leukemia had to miss a treatment because the drug was unavailable . Other children might have to miss treatments in coming weeks , say officials there . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The shortage of tamoxifen will be more widely felt . Around 9,000 people receive it through Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s public drug plan . Many more who are not in the public plan are also prescribed the drug , which is one of the most common cancer treatments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A kind of hormone treatment therapy , tamoxifen is used to treat breast cancer in patients whose cancer is hormone receptor positive . It works by interfering with the effects of estrogen in the breast tissue and is often prescribed to patients after surgery . Patients usually take it daily for five to 10 years . It is also sometimes used to reduce the chances of breast cancer in high-risk patients as well as in patients with metastatic cancer as well as in some other cancers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It has been on the market for more than 30 years and can reduce cancer recurrence after surgery by nearly 50 per cent , said Forbes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health Canada has been working to obtain other supplies of the drug after two of the three suppliers to Canada experienced production problems that led to shortages . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Forbes said she is aware of some patients showing up at their pharmacy and being given a smaller supply of pills than their prescription calls for and some pharmacists calling around to try and obtain more supply . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She suggested that patients who have been unable to fill their prescriptions contact their oncologist or family doctor to find an alternative that can be used until tamoxifen is available . It is better for patients to see their doctors and try to find an alternative , she said , rather than going without . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We try to make sure patients get the treatment they need . So if they ran out of their pills and they couldn&amp;rsquo ; t take them for many months then that might be a significant impact , but we are hoping that is not going to be the case because we think the shortage will be shorter than that . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , hospital pharmacies are working to source or find alternatives to a growing list of drugs on back order in Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The Ottawa Hospital&amp;rsquo ; s pharmacy team works diligently with clinicians in monitoring the supply for a number of drugs , to ensure that we have an adequate supply , &amp;rdquo ; said spokesperson Michaela Schreiter. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When supply for a particular drug becomes low , they look for alternative suppliers first , followed by other drugs in a similar class , then alternative treatments , when necessary . This has allowed us to maintain quality of care for patients . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Forbes , who herself treats breast cancer patients , said many of them are anxious about the drug shortage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The last thing we want is for patients to feel anxious about not being able to obtain their medication . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; epayne@postmedia.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21724;TOOLONG ... reducing your carbon footprint all wrong : The merits of one less child&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21759;TOOLONG ... case for getting fitter -- not slimmer : Why our obsession with weight could be a mistake&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;21794;TOOLONG ... of RCMP officer who helped lead fight against sexual misconduct is denied compensation&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneTue , 12 Nov 2019 11:57:29 **45;21829;TOOLONG ...
