NewsWomenA century of trauma : Tracing the evolution of PTSD through four soldiershttp : **32;22232;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;22266;TOOLONG ... title= " Pte . Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " alt= " Pte . Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;22302;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500695 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the opening morning of the Battle of Vimy Ridge , Capt . Thain MacDowell ran towards enemy lines through a welter of mud and craters , sleet and machine gunfire . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He reached his objective , a German trench , only to find that he had become separated from most of his company . Joined by a pair of army couriers , MacDowell captured two machine gun placements , then climbed down a flight of steps into a deep dugout . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Around a sharp corner , he confronted a roomful of German soldiers . He turned and shouted to an imaginary group of Canadians behind him to hold their grenades . Seventy-seven Germans surrendered . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;22332;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;22374;TOOLONG ... The latest treatment **28;22409;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;22439;TOOLONG ... War army nurse enlisted out of concern for her **28;22474;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;22504;TOOLONG ... composer sets veteran 's poem to music for Remembrance Day&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;22539;TOOLONG ... Alex Kowbel typed his way into the **29;22574;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; He sent the prisoners up the stairs in groups of 12 to conceal the fact they were surrendering to just three Canadian soldiers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They had plenty of rations but we had a great time taking them prisoner , &amp;rdquo ; MacDowell wrote in a dispatch later that day , April 9 , 1917. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His act of courage and deception would earn him the British Empire&amp;rsquo ; s highest decoration for military valour . One of four Canadians awarded the Victoria Cross at Vimy Ridge , MacDowell was the only one still alive six months later when he returned home to Brockville on sick leave . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell was not sick in the conventional sense : He was suffering from what military doctors called &amp;ldquo ; war neurasthenia , &amp;rdquo ; or shellshock . His symptoms included depression , insomnia , headaches , irritability , fever , perspiration , difficulty concentrating and decreased energy . He also had a slight speech impediment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell was one of 10,000 Canadian soldiers diagnosed with shellshock during the First World War . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The condition baffled doctors and challenged military leaders , who didn&amp;rsquo ; t know how to deal with the flood of traumatized soldiers that accompanied every major battle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some attributed the phenomenon to emotional weakness or malingering . More than 300 British and Commonwealth soldiers were executed for cowardice or desertion during the war , including 23 Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An unknown number of them suffered from what today we would call post-traumatic stress disorder ( PTSD ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; War has inflicted trauma on successive generations of Canadian soldiers whose psychiatric injuries have been variously labelled shellshock , battle exhaustion , combat stress reaction and PTSD . The evolution of that diagnosis has traced a century of conflict : It is a story of service and science and suffering . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;22605;TOOLONG ... title= " First World War Victoria Cross winner Lt.-Col. Thain MacDowell. " alt= " First World War Victoria Cross winner Lt.-Col. Thain MacDowell. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;22641;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500700 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Capt . Thain MacDowell&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In February 1915 , British psychologist Dr. Charles Myers was the first to identify the phenomenon of shellshock . In the medical journal The Lancet , &lt;a href= " https : **33;22671;TOOLONG ... recounted the case histories of three soldiers&lt;/a&gt; traumatized by shell explosions . Curiously , he said , the soldiers&amp;rsquo ; hearing was little affected , while other functions such as sight , smell , taste and memory were damaged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The close relation of these cases to those of &amp;lsquo ; hysteria&amp;rsquo ; appears fairly certain , &amp;rdquo ; he concluded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hysteria was a mental disorder , attributed mostly to women at the time , which typically featured nervousness , fainting or fits . Shellshocked soldiers could be rendered mute or left with partially paralyzed limbs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some doctors theorized that shellshock was the result of a physical brain injury caused by soldiers&amp;rsquo ; repeated exposure to blast waves from exploding shells &amp;mdash ; a new part of industrialized warfare . Others pointed to afflicted soldiers who had never been in an explosion to argue that the condition was due to a weakness of the nervous system , &amp;ldquo ; neurasthenia , &amp;rdquo ; triggered by the general stress of war . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The world&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;a href= " https : **33;22706;TOOLONG ... personality test&lt;/a&gt; was developed in an attempt to identify recruits with the &amp;ldquo ; emotional instability&amp;rdquo ; that could put them at risk for shellshock. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Treatments were mostly experimental , and sometimes , horrifying . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In December 1916 , Myers spearheaded the establishment of specialized medical units near the frontlines to assess and treat traumatized soldiers using Freudian talk therapy . Theorizing that shellshock was a stress disorder , he believed a patient had to relive his experience to reintegrate the traumatic event with his conscious mind . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A Canadian psychiatrist , Dr. Lewis Yealland , was the leading proponent of an altogether different school of thought : that shellshock was a kind of personal failure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Yealland , a clinician at London&amp;rsquo ; s National Hospital for the Paralyzed and Epileptic , was convinced he could recondition traumatized soldiers through the power of suggestion . He regularly accompanied those suggestions with powerful electric shocks , and sometimes , cigarette burns . He used electrotherapy on 196 patients during the war , and published his results in a disturbing 1918 book , &lt;a href= " https : **33;22741;TOOLONG ... Disorders of Warfare&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; No one , including Yealland , could suggest that war hero Thain MacDowell lacked battlefield courage or personal fortitude . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Awarded the Victoria Cross in June 1917 , MacDowell was hospitalized in England and sent home to Canada in October . He spent three months at Brockville General Hospital where , &lt;a href= " http : **30;22776;TOOLONG ? op= ... to his medical history&lt;/a&gt; , he suffered a nervous breakdown . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In January 1918 , after a period of rest , he was deemed fit for service again : &amp;ldquo ; Officer shows much improvement since last examination &amp;mdash ; has regained his emotional control . No attacks of crying since Nov. 17. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell returned to England in February 1918 , and spent the year in officer training as the First World War raced towards its bloody conclusion . He returned to Canada in December , one month after the armistice , and again sought help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A medical history taken at the time says : &amp;ldquo ; Officer states that he tires easily and can not sleep . Has not slept well since Nov. 1916 . He may sleep 3 to 4 hours a night if there has been no excitement . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; ( In November 1916 , MacDowell was thrown into the air by a shell blast at the Somme ; he earned the Distinguished Service Order for his role in capturing three machine gun posts during the same battle. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In January 1919 , MacDowell was made commanding officer of a demobilization unit in Ottawa , where he was also an outpatient at the Sir Sandford Fleming Convalescent Home . He could only manage the work for a few months . By August 1919 , he was an in-patient at Montreal&amp;rsquo ; s Ste. Anne de Bellevue Hospital , complaining of depression , insomnia , restlessness and irritability. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He tires very easily and in all work loses interest , &amp;rdquo ; reads his medical case history . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Montreal , he was prescribed massage and hydrotherapy , a popular method for treating mental illness in the early 20th century . Warm , continuous baths were used to treat agitated patients ; they were often bathed in a darkened room for hours , sometimes days , at a time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In October 1919 , after MacDowell was deemed medically unfit for service and discharged , he returned to Ottawa , where he slowly recovered his mental health . His military file does not disclose what treatment he received . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For five years , he worked as private secretary to the minister of defence , and in 1929 , married Norah Hodgson , of Montreal . They had two sons . He later entered the mining business as an investor and executive . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell died of a heart attack in March 1960 . He was 69. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;22808;TOOLONG ... title= " Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " alt= " Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;22844;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500685 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Signalman William " Ted " Patrick &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the Second World War , signalmen maintained communication links between frontline officers and headquarter staff who managed the battlefield. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Enemy forces regularly used signalmen &amp;mdash ; they carried radios on their backs &amp;mdash ; to aim their artillery since they knew officers would be nearby . It made Signalmen William &amp;ldquo ; Ted&amp;rdquo ; Patrick a target in 1944 as he fought his way north through Italy with the Irish Regiment of Canada . He suffered perforated eardrums from shells exploding so close to him . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patrick&amp;rsquo ; s Italian campaign had other harrowing moments . In the Moro River Valley , he saw a heavily pregnant woman ripped open by a landmine . During another advance , he had to cover the lighted dials of his radio as German soldiers walked past him into an ambush. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He did not seek help for the profound anxiety he suffered . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Infantry soldiers like Patrick were the primary victims of &amp;ldquo ; battle exhaustion&amp;rdquo ; in the Second World War . Research by Canadian military historian Terry Copp , a professor at Wilfrid Laurier University , found that 90 per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s battle exhaustion cases came from ground troops . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In part , that was a reflection of the Royal Canadian Air Force&amp;rsquo ; s uncompromising attitude towards aircrew members who developed psychiatric problems and refused to fly . Such airmen were branded as &amp;ldquo ; lacking in moral fibre&amp;rdquo ; or LMF ; they were often demoted or dishonourably discharged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canadian army took a more pragmatic view . Its senior psychiatrist , Col. Frederick Van Nostrand , wanted battle exhausted soldiers treated quickly while close to the frontlines so they could be promptly returned to action . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It meant that as Canadian forces fought through Normandy , hundreds of soldiers were treated each week at field dressing stations for acute battle stress . Typically , they were sedated for 24 hours , given two days of rest , and counselled by a therapist . Many were returned to action only to suffer another breakdown . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Battle exhaustion cases represented one-quarter of all wounded soldiers among Allied forces . &amp;nbsp ; Those numbers caught military planners by surprise in Canada , where medical officers had tried to weed out recruits with emotional instability . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The methods that were used were no better than flipping a coin , &amp;rdquo ; Copp , the author of two books on the history of combat stress , said in an interview . &amp;ldquo ; None of it worked in terms of predicting who would break down or who would not break down under conditions of combat . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a prophetic report filed at the end of the war , Van Nostrand said he was unsure doctors would ever solve &amp;ldquo ; the vast problem of the psychiatric breakdown of soldiers during war . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It is my opinion , &amp;rdquo ; he wrote , &amp;ldquo ; that the methods now employed in the British , American , and Canadian armies will not materially lower the incidence of psychiatric casualties in a fighting force . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are various reasons for these opinions but two of them are fundamental : First , there is direct conflict between the needs of the service and the needs of the individual soldier as assessed by his physician . Secondly , the attitudes and behaviour of the successful soldier are contrary to most of his previous teaching . He must not allow death or mutilation of his comrades to prevent him from reaching his objective , and finally , he must pretend that he is glad to risk his life for that cause . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Van Nostrand pleaded with military planners to accept that normal people can not always manage the exceptional stress of war . &amp;ldquo ; Every soldier has his breaking point , &amp;rdquo ; he warned . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ted Patrick had bumped up against his breaking point . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;22874;TOOLONG ... title= " Ted Patrick . " alt= " Ted Patrick . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;22910;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500684 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; After the Second World War , Patrick returned home to Ottawa and buried his memories . It was a common approach . He married , took a job in the civil service , and launched a bee-keeping business to supplement his income . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; All the while , however , the tide of war washed over his subconscious . Patrick sometimes attacked his wife in the middle of the night , believing her to be an enemy soldier ; she eventually began to sleep in a separate bedroom . Other times , he&amp;rsquo ; d wake up sobbing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patrick scrupulously avoided the legion hall and regimental reunions &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; anything that brought the war to mind . He was also extremely cautious . He didn&amp;rsquo ; t like to go to unfamiliar places ; he was , he said , like a rat that stayed close to a wall . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I would not take a chance on getting hurt or having the family hurt . I was always extremely cautious and went around danger , &amp;rdquo ; he once told an interviewer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t until the 1980s that Patrick was finally diagnosed with PTSD ; his psychiatrist urged him to confront his wartime trauma . Talking about his experiences &amp;mdash ; and sharing his memories &amp;mdash ; eased Patrick&amp;rsquo ; s anxiety . Late in life , he became a dedicated volunteer at the Canadian War Museum and travelled to Holland for ceremonies to commemorate the country&amp;rsquo ; s liberation . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He died in February 2015. &lt;strong&gt; &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;22940;TOOLONG ... title= " Gordon Forbes poses for a photo in his home in Ottawa Tuesday Oct 29 , 2019. " alt= " Gordon Forbes poses for a photo in his home in Ottawa Tuesday Oct 29 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;22976;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500678 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Lt . Gordon Forbes &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Gordon Forbes , 76 , of Orl&amp;eacute ; ans , was on board &lt;a href= " http : **34;23006;TOOLONG ... Kootenay&lt;/a&gt; 50 years ago during the worst peacetime disaster in the history of the Royal Canadian Navy &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; an event that would colour much of his life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On Oct. 23 , 1969 , H.M.C.S. Kootenay was in the North Atlantic , returning to Halifax from a NATO naval exercise . At 8:21 a.m. , during a full power trial &amp;mdash ; a drill to test the destroyer&amp;rsquo ; s performance at top speed &amp;mdash ; an explosion ripped through the ship&amp;rsquo ; s engine room . A mass of flames shot from a broken gearbox , setting fire to the 10 men inside of the room . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Only three escaped alive . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thick black smoke quickly filled the lower decks , but its source wasn&amp;rsquo ; t readily apparent to those on the bridge , including Lt. Gordon Forbes , the ship&amp;rsquo ; s weapons officer who was responsible for Kootenay&amp;rsquo ; s 50 tonnes of ammunition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Engineering Officer Al Kennedy , one of those to escape the engine room , stumbled into the bridge , blackened and badly burned : &amp;ldquo ; Fire in the engine room , &amp;rdquo ; he announced . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That posed problems . The ship&amp;rsquo ; s firefighting equipment was stored near the engine room , and the ship&amp;rsquo ; s main ammunition magazine was immediately behind it . A sailor reported the bulkhead between the two was already hot . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Divers donned tanks and masks to descend into the smoke : They retrieved the ship&amp;rsquo ; s firefighting equipment and rescued sailors trapped by the blinding smoke . Forbes sprayed down the magazine to reduce the threat of a catastrophic explosion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If the magazine had blown up , it would have destroyed the ship , &amp;rdquo ; he told this newspaper . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It took about three hours to bring the fire under control ; the magazine was then flooded to better stabilize the munitions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Those on board were told not to talk about the disaster , which had killed nine of their fellow sailors . &amp;ldquo ; No one really knew how to deal with it , &amp;rdquo ; said Forbes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the time of the Kootenay disaster , the Vietnam War was in full swing : In 1969 , the number of deployed U.S. troops peaked at 549,000. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23042;TOOLONG ... title= " HMCS Kootenay approaching flight locks , Welland canal . " alt= " HMCS Kootenay approaching flight locks , Welland canal . " data-portal-copyright= " CF Photo Unit " **28;23078;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500686 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Curiously , few soldiers reported battle fatigue symptoms in Vietnam . Army officials attributed that development to limited battlefield exposure : Soldiers were rotated through the war on one-year tours of duty . It gave them a firm date by which their wartime ordeal would end . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many military planners thought the problem of battlefield stress injuries had been solved . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , of course , it had simply gone to ground . Tens of thousands of soldiers returned from Vietnam traumatized : afflicted by nightmares , insomnia , depression , rage , paranoia and addictions . Psychiatrists labeled the phenomenon delayed psychiatric trauma or &amp;ldquo ; post-Vietnam Syndrome&amp;rdquo ; since some thought the disorder was unique to Vietnam . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was the first time that psychiatrists recognized that stress injuries were not always immediate , but could announce themselves months , even years , later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Psychiatrists who worked with Vietnam veterans lobbied to have the disorder formally recognized , and in 1980 , the authoritative American Psychiatric Association made PTSD part of its Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The formal recognition of PTSD had profound consequences and allowed for better diagnosis and treatment . Therapists recognized the same disorder in Holocaust survivors , sexual assault victims , first responders &amp;mdash ; and others afflicted by traumatic events such as the Kootenay explosion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sub-Lieut . Clark Reiffenstein , one of those who donned scuba gear to plunge into the ship&amp;rsquo ; s smoke-filled lower decks , died of suicide one month after the fire . He was posthumously awarded the Star of Courage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many other Kootenay sailors struggled with alcoholism , nightmares and anxiety . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 1990 , Gordon Forbes was diagnosed with clinical depression soon after retiring from the navy . He suffered from paranoia and had difficulty sleeping . His condition was later linked to PTSD and recognized as a service injury by Veterans Affairs Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was one measure of the advance in the military&amp;rsquo ; s approach to psychiatric infirmity . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; I was very pleased that they started to recognize PTSD , &amp;rdquo ; he said , &amp;ldquo ; and not just throw people out of the service on medical grounds , which is what happened to people who went to get help after the Kootenay fire . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2010 , Forbes published a book , We Are As One , about the disaster and its emotional aftermath . Researching and writing the book , he said , was a cathartic experience for everyone involved : &amp;ldquo ; I had so many men come up to me after I wrote the book and say , &amp;lsquo ; I thought I was the only one . ' &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23108;TOOLONG ... title= " Natacha Dupuis is a former Canadian soldier and Afghan vet who suffered debilitating PTSD after her war service . " alt= " Natacha Dupuis is a former Canadian soldier and Afghan vet who suffered debilitating PTSD after her war service . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;23144;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500687 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Master Cpl . Natacha Dupuis&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ten years ago , in March 2009 , Master Cpl . Natacha Dupuis was put in charge of her first mission with the reconnaissance squadron of the Royal Canadian Dragoons : a week-long foot patrol in Kandahar Province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Qualified as a tank gunner , she had served in Bosnia and was on her second tour of duty in Afghanistan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leaving the Forward Operating Base Frontenac , a military outpost near Kandahar , Dupuis led her patrol to a hilltop camp . The next morning , as the patrol departed , a massive explosion ripped into the armoured vehicle behind Dupuis&amp;rsquo ; vehicle . The 14-tonne Coyote was blown into the air and landed on its roof . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dupuis helped to collect the remains of two dead soldiers while preparing for a secondary attack that never came . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her team was quickly evacuated , but Dupuis kept reliving the incident and re-imagining the terrible scene . For days , unable to turn off her flow of adrenaline , she couldn&amp;rsquo ; t sleep . A psychiatrist prescribed her sleeping pills , but she struggled through each day and often sought out a private place to cry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She willed herself through her final two months of service in Afghanistan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As soon as she returned home to Petawawa , however , she fell apart : Dupuis suffered powerful flashbacks and panic attacks that left her gasping for air . Diagnosed with PTSD , she transferred to Ottawa , then took a leave . She left the military for good in 2014. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her story is a familiar one . A &lt;a href= " https : **33;23174;TOOLONG ... Affairs Canada report last year&lt;/a&gt; revealed that about 16 per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Afghan veterans &amp;mdash ; more than 6,700 soldiers &amp;mdash ; have been diagnosed with PTSD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The PTSD rate remained high in Afghanistan even though the military had tried to carefully prepare soldiers for the stress of war . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Soldiers were briefed about the nature of stress injuries and the importance of seeking early treatment . Those leaving Afghanistan were given an overseas decompression period and repeatedly screened for PTSD or related afflictions . But the &amp;ldquo ; psychological inoculation&amp;rdquo ; of soldiers did little to reduce the overall incidence of PTSD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I personally feel I was absolutely ready to face going to Afghanistan , &amp;rdquo ; said Dupuis. &amp;ldquo ; I was given very good training and it showed . She co-captained Team Canada at the 2017 Invictus Games in Toronto , and won three gold medals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; For me , I think the big breakthrough came with sport &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; but I had to be ready for that breakthrough , &amp;rdquo ; Dupuis said . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a very complex recovery process . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although she still suffers the occasional flashback &amp;mdash ; fireworks or big crowds can trigger them &amp;mdash ; Dupuis has returned to work as a peer support co-ordinator with Operational Stress Injury Social Support , a joint program of Veterans Affairs Canada and the Department of National Defence . She helps soldiers and veterans with PTSD. &amp;ldquo ; I share my experience , &amp;rdquo ; she said , &amp;ldquo ; and try to give them hope that it is possible to have a better life . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s most decorated soldiers have suffered the effects of PTSD , including &lt;a href= " https : **33;23244;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " Peter Bregg " **28;23385;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500698 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; It underlines the fact that a century after shellshock was first described in a medical journal , doctors still can&amp;rsquo ; t predict who will suffer PTSD when exposed to the horrors of war , or why some soldiers are affected and not others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Through statistical analysis , researchers know women are more likely than men to develop PTSD ; that people with pre-existing psychiatric conditions are more vulnerable ; and that risk increases with each additional overseas deployment a soldier undertakes. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Scientists are also slowly coming to understand what actually happens in the brain of those with PTSD : Research suggests the amygdala , an almond-shaped region of the brain that processes emotions , is overactive along with parts of the prefrontal cortex that promote fear . " alt= " Veronika Sedlakova , post-doctoral fellow ( L ) , Sarah Mclaughlin , PhD(c) , and Dr. Emilio Alarcon , principal investigator and laboratory director , University of Ottawa Heart Institute , have developed a recombinant human collagen matrix for cardiac tissue repair . " data-portal-copyright= " Errol McGihon " **28;23840;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1491854 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; It took years for Emilio Alarcon and his University of Ottawa Heart Institute research team to fully believe what they were seeing &amp;mdash ; that a gel they had developed containing human collagen was repairing damaged hearts in mice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They repeated their research study several times , coming up with randomized , blinded results , just to make sure the findings were correct . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We had to complete it many times because we couldn&amp;rsquo ; t believe it , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The results of that work , five years in the making , were published in the prestigious journal Nature Communications on Friday . Alarcon and Erik Suuronen , a scientist in the division of cardiac surgery and director of its biomaterials and regeneration program , are lead authors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The injectable material is the first in the world prepared using human collagen and is being called an unprecedented leap forward in addressing repair of cardiac muscle after a heart attack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The work is still years away from clinical use on humans , but the findings are expected to attract attention because of the potential of the gel , which is designed to be injected into the hearts of patients with damaged heart tissue after a heart attack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alarcon said his team believes it performs better than any of the cell-based therapies or drug treatments currently available . The treatment works , he said , by increasing the number of cardiac muscle cells and blood capillaries in the tissue around damaged areas of the heart . The gel also helps bring more wound-healing cells to the site to promote repair . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Heart diseases are the leading cause of death around the world , and coronary artery disease , which can lead to a heart attack , is the most common . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; About 10 per cent of people who have a heart attack ( or myocardial infarction ) will develop scarring and thickening of the heart wall that can lead to heart failure , which has a high mortality rate and its treatment is costly to the health system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alarcon noted that patients in remote areas without easy access to health care and those who don&amp;rsquo ; t seek immediate treatment or don&amp;rsquo ; t know they had a heart attack are more likely to suffer heart muscle damage . The treatment being developed by the heart institute team restored heart function in mice with scarred cardiac muscle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The heart institute&amp;rsquo ; s BioEngineering and Therapeutic Solutions ( BEaTS ) team &amp;ldquo ; are hopeful their human collagen gel will one day lead to a recovery of heart function and prevent heart failure in humans , &amp;rdquo ; said Alarcon , &amp;ldquo ; but more testing is required . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study published Friday is a first step toward that potential treatment , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Canada , approximately 600,000 patients live with advanced heart failure and health-care costs amount to more than $2.8 billion every year . The elderly and frail are increasingly collateral damage in the drive to end hallway medicine in Ontario , say advocates and families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patients who occupy hospital beds but no longer need acute care , ALC &amp;mdash ; alternative level of care &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; patients are a key factor in hospital overcrowding . But with record waiting lists for long-term care beds and shortages of home care workers , patients and their families say they are caught in the middle and feeling pressured. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This is a crisis , &amp;rdquo ; said Melanie Dea of Rockland , who recently experienced that pressure first hand . Her husband Richard Martin , who has Huntington&amp;rsquo ; s disease , was treated at Montfort Hospital for pneumonia in July . By August he had improved , but was on a waiting list for long-term care and Dea could not safely care for him at home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said the hospital suggested he go to an Alzheimer&amp;rsquo ; s unit of a long-term care home . Rea refused because her husband does not have dementia . The hospital began charging him $62.18 a day , a co-payment she says she will not pay . He has since moved to a long-term care home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the wife of an elderly patient in the same hospital room was in tears after being told her husband was being discharged , said Dea . The man ended up in the hospital because he was wandering the streets at night and his wife could no longer care for him . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Trevor Mertz of Chesterville , says his mother-in-law felt pressured to move into an Ottawa long-term care home by staff at Winchester Hospital when she was there in 2017. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They said , &amp;lsquo ; You have two hours to decide or the spot will be gone . ' &amp;rdquo ; Her stay at the home , with a history of health and safety violations , was a &amp;ldquo ; nightmare&amp;rdquo ; , according to Mertz . If I had seen the place , I would have said no. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jane Meadus of the Toronto-based Advocacy Centre for the Elderly said her organization hears from families on a daily basis who are distraught about having to quickly find a solution for a frail relative being discharged from hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They come to us in tears . The preference , though , is for them to apply from home . &amp;ldquo ; Research has demonstrated that it is easier for people to make important decisions for the next stage while they are in their regular environment and can validate if they can safely remain in their home . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said she is aware of cases in which people have felt pressured to leave , but added patients will get better care tailored to their needs at home with service providers , in a retirement home or long-term care home . &amp;ldquo ; We know that situations such as these are stressful times for the patients and their loved ones . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leah Levesque , head of nursing at Queensway Carleton Hospital , acknowledged that the transition from hospital to home or institutional care can be hard on families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think the bottom line for us is we think patients should be in the right bed getting appropriate care from the most appropriate providers . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That can be easier said than done , though . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The average wait in the Ottawa area for long-term care was 186 days in 2017 , above the provincial average of 146 days . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;24345;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1482574 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When the treatment was done , the patient looked confused . &amp;ldquo ; Is that it ? &amp;rdquo ; he asked Dr. Calum Redpath. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That was it . The potentially lifesaving treatment for a deadly heart ailment was completed in a painless , non-invasive session . The patient was free to go . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Performed by a team of doctors from the University of Ottawa Heart Institute in partnership with doctors at The Ottawa Hospital cancer centre , the treatment done in late September was a first in Canada . The Heart Institute is now one of the few centres in the world capable of performing it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This new technique offers patients a treatment option that does not require the body to be opened in any way , &amp;rdquo ; Redpath said . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a real game-changing innovation , almost a fairytale . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although it is still experimental and being offered on a compassionate basis , Redpath believes the &amp;ldquo ; sky is the limit&amp;rdquo ; for the ways the procedure could change treatment of a common and often deadly heart arrhythmia called ventricular tachycardia , including enabling it to be performed on more patients in smaller centres using equipment used to treat cancer patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;24375;TOOLONG ... title= " The team behind the breakthrough procedure in Ottawa includes , left to right , Professor of Cardiology Dr. Andrew Crean , Associate Professor of Cardiology Dr. Calum Redpath , medical physicist Katie Lekx-Toniolo and Radiation Oncologist Dr. Graham Cook . " alt= " The team behind the breakthrough procedure in Ottawa includes , left to right , Professor of Cardiology Dr. Andrew Crean , Associate Professor of Cardiology Dr. Calum Redpath , medical physicist Katie Lekx-Toniolo and Radiation Oncologist Dr. Graham Cook . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;24411;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1482623 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sudden cardiac death kills around 50,000 Canadians every year . Most of those deaths are caused by ventricular arrhythmia , the condition that is the focus of the new non-invasive treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Conventional treatment for ventricular arrhythmia involves surgery : usually through a catheter inserted in an artery or vein in the patient&amp;rsquo ; s groin . Once inside , radio-frequency energy or other methods are used to destroy the damaged area of the patient&amp;rsquo ; s heart muscle that is causing rapid and irregular heartbeats . That ablation , as it is known , is done to restore a regular heartbeat . More than 150 such surgeries are performed at the Heart Institute every year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The new non-invasive procedure first performed in Ottawa last month could end the need for traditional heart surgery to treat the common and often deadly heart arrhythmia . Instead of time in an operating room , anesthesia , pain medicine and days of hospitalization and recovery , the patient who underwent the treatment last month put his shirt back on and walked home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Current drug treatment for the condition are either ineffective or have side-effects , and the invasive procedures , including catheter ablation surgery or implanting a defibrillator , require prolonged surgery with potential complications and sometimes long recoveries. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The procedure that uses two novel therapies , took place in late September . First , the patient underwent electrocardiographic imaging , in which doctors mapped the electrical activity of his heart using advanced imaging technology . During that procedure , the patient was fully awake and conscious , said Dr. Andrew Crean , co-director of the cardiac MRI service at the Heart Institute . He works with Redpath to identify damaged heart tissue causing arrhythmias. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Using that map , a radiation oncologist burned off damaged areas of the heart muscle using technology normally used to treat cancer patients . No surgery was needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re excited to use this treatment now on portions of the heart , with the hope that , with just one 30-minute treatment , our current patients will live longer and eventually contribute to research studies so we can learn more about who can benefit the most from this and by how much , said Dr. Graham Cook , a radiation oncologist working on the treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Redpath says he expects up to six patients to receive the treatment in Ottawa in coming months . They are all patients who are unable or unwilling to pursue conventional treatments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So far , 30 patients have been treated , mostly through Washington University in St. Louis , where it was developed . Among those patients , there is a 94 per cent success rate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But , before it can be widely used , the treatment will be studied to determine whether it is worthwhile . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Redpath said the procedure is significantly less costly than conventional treatment &amp;mdash ; maybe five times less than surgery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If it were to become a routine treatment , he said , it could change how many patients were treated by allowing smaller hospitals to treat patients , even using it as a preventative procedure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The sky is the limit . The vaccine is now licensed to pharmaceutical company Merck , which is in the process of getting it approved and regulated . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , it is being used during the Ebola outbreak in the DRC on a compassionate basis . So far , more than 2,000 people have died in what is the second-worst Ebola outbreak the world has seen , after the West African outbreak , which lasted from 2014 until 2016. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nickerson , who has recently returned to Ottawa from DRC , said Doctors Without Borders wants to see more transparency around how the vaccine is being rolled out by the World Health Organization there . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; For a long time , one of the big problems with this vaccine is that there has been very little transparency into many aspects of it . The technique was used to eradicate smallpox . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nickerson said the strategy is rigid . These investments will fund transportation infrastructure , water and wastewater facilities , as well as education and social infrastructure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Not included on that list ? Health care infrastructure . In fact , hospitals have been explicitly excluded from accessing Infrastructure Canada&amp;rsquo ; s funding programs for more than a decade . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s innovation programs &amp;ndash ; whether administered via Innovation Canada or through the Canada Foundation for Innovation ( CFI ) &amp;ndash ; select against leadership by health care providers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Innovation Canada favours industry leadership , both in its Innovative Superclusters Initiative and through its Strategic Innovation Fund and tends to relegate health care organizations to a supporting role . Meanwhile , CFI requires that any hospital application have sign-off from the president of a university , whose priorities are likely to lie elsewhere . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Why do we do this ? Why do we design these programs in ways that make it either difficult or impossible for hospitals , researchers and patients to benefit ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some may argue that federalism stands in the way ; that anything that happens in a hospital is outside the scope of the federal government , but that is incorrect . In fact , the federal Hospital Construction Grant Program that ran from 1948 to 1970 was the financial engine that built the current hospital infrastructure . Unfortunately , that engine has sputtered to a halt . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canadian voters must hold the federal government responsible for the care and maintenance of the hospitals it helped to create . Many of these institutions are now desperately in need of renewal even as demand increases due to our growing and aging population . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nearly half of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s hospitals are more than 50 years old and it is impossible to expect 21st-century medicine in a building designed for care models of a half a century ago . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our aging hospital infrastructure also has the unfortunate side effect of consuming approximately 11 per cent of total public energy and accounting collectively for more than five per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s greenhouse gas footprint . Not only is modern hospital infrastructure important for providing better care , it is also a much greener solution . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In late July , among many other similar announcements , the federal government pledged $1 million to provide much-needed upgrades to 46-year old Blackburn Arena in Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s east end . A coalition of six community health centres are at the centre of the Ottawa proposal , which also includes The Ottawa Hospital , Bruy&amp;egrave ; re , Ottawa Inner City Health , Carefor and Ottawa Public Health , along with numerous other organizations , totalling 47 partners . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two other Ottawa-area teams have also received green lights to move forward : one focused on children&amp;rsquo ; s health that includes CHEO and more than 50 other members , including Eastern Ontario hospitals ; and one in the city&amp;rsquo ; s east end that includes the Montfort Hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The province announced last spring it would call for groups to form health teams as part of a major revamp of the provincial health system . The Ontario government is in the process of disbanding the LHIN ( local health integration ) system and has concentrated most health organizations in the province into a central agency . LHINs are to be replaced by health teams , which are meant to co-ordinate care among various health organizations . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health Minister Christine Elliott has said the system will offer &amp;ldquo ; seamless access to health services , including primary care , hospitals , home and community care , palliative care , residential long-term care and mental health and addictions service . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;26751;TOOLONG ... title= " Ontario Health Minister Christine Elliott in a file photo from August . He also wondered whether hospital-driven health teams might be able to &amp;ldquo ; resist the temptation to consolidate regional budgets to gradually provide better hospital funding ? &amp;rdquo ; He noted hospital budgets have been squeezed in recent years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But those at the centre of planning for the Ottawa Health Team say there is genuine excitement about the prospect of doing things in a different , more streamlined way . We are about having the right care , at the right time , with the right provider . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thibault said the team would focus on primary care and preventative care and medicine , as well as acute care . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the aim of the team to to help fill gaps in the transitions between different types of care , she said . &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneMon , 09 Sep 2019 13:57:12 **45;26988;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal NewsMenSeniorsWomenWomen more likely to die after bypass surgery : Ontario studyhttp : **35;27035;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;27072;TOOLONG ... title= " Files : Cardiogram monitor in surgery " alt= " Files : Cardiogram monitor in surgery " data-portal-copyright= " Fotolia " **28;27108;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 813971 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Women are more likely than men to die after cardiac surgery , a study of more than 72,000 Ontario cardiac patients has found . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study , which was recently published in the Journal of the American Heart Association , found that women were more likely to die than men after coronary artery bypass surgery or valve surgery ( including combined surgeries ) within 30 days as well as in the longer term . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study , conducted by researchers at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute and the University Health Network in Toronto , adds to mounting evidence that heart disease is different in women than in men and that sometimes women&amp;rsquo ; s health suffers as a result . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Research at the Heart Institute and elsewhere , as well as campaigns for patients and health professionals , have helped raise awareness about this and to avoid heart problems going untreated or being overlooked in women . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Louise Sun , a cardiac anesthesiologist and clinical scientist at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute , and author of the study , said being female is a &amp;ldquo ; statistically significant risk factor for dying after surgery . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Researchers followed 72,824 Ontario patients who had undergone cardiac bypass and valve surgeries between October 1 , 2008 and December 31 , 2016 . The majority of patients were men &amp;mdash ; reflecting the fact that more men than women suffer from heart disease . Twenty five per cent of the patients were women . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Women had significantly higher rates of death than men after coronary artery bypass surgery and combined bypass surgery and mitral valve surgery . Women had lower rates of long-term mortality after isolated mitral valve replacement , although men had lower death rates after isolated mitral valve repair . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The findings were enough for researchers to find that merely being female is associated with &amp;ldquo ; long-term mortality&amp;rdquo ; after cardiac surgery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sun pointed to several reasons for women&amp;rsquo ; s high death rates after some cardiac surgery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One is that women tend to be older than men when they require cardiac bypass surgery , are more frail and more medically complex than men , often with other health issues such as diabetes and hypertension. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In addition , women often experience a delay in treatment compared to men , which means their conditions tend to be more serious when they undergo surgery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These established sex differences explain our overall observation of lower estimated long-term survival in women after cardiac surgery and of female sex being an independent risk factor for long-term mortality . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sun said that among the medical complexities in female patients is the likelihood that some of those undergoing bypass and mitral valve surgery have had a previous heart attack that has been missed . That could explain why they needed surgery to replace a leaky mitral valve . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although there has been a focus on the need for more research and awareness about women&amp;rsquo ; s heart health in recent years , the study&amp;rsquo ; s results suggest a gap still remains . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Given the substantial sex differences in patient presentation for coronary and valvular heart disease , further efforts need to be directed at the education of both physicians and patients in the early recognition of acute presentation of cardiac disease in women , &amp;rdquo ; the authors wrote . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is also a need for sex specific risk prediction models for patients undergoing cardiac surgery , something Sun said is in the works . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While the findings are significant , Sun noted that the risk of dying after bypass surgery remains very low , in the one-per-cent range , &amp;ldquo ; but out of that one per cent we are seeing more women than men . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;27138;TOOLONG " **34;27167;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27203;TOOLONG ... critically injured in Orl ? ans dies in Israeli hospital&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27238;TOOLONG ... girl continues life-saving treatment as third bone marrow registry clinic planned&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27273;TOOLONG ... called into deaths of Basil Borustki 's three murder victims&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneThu , 29 Aug 2019 12:59:24 **45;27308;TOOLONG ... NewsWomenCold storage : The promise of Ottawa 's cord blood bankhttp : **36;27355;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;27393;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " alt= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;27429;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448089 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;27459;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Inside two high-tech tanks filled with liquid nitrogen in an industrial park in Nepean there are about 2,500 little bags of frozen stem cells . The contents of each one of these little bags has the potential to save a life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The &amp;ldquo ; **26;27495;TOOLONG ; freezers contain blood harvested from the umbilical cords and placentas of newborn babies , many of them in Ottawa . The immature stem cells in cord blood are used to treat more than 80 diseases , most frequently blood cancers and other blood disorders such as leukemia , lymphoma , aplastic anemia and sickle cell disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are other possible treatments in the pipeline . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the future , stem cells might be used to treat a broad range of diseases , from diabetes to Parkinson&amp;rsquo ; s , multiple sclerosis and &amp;mdash ; this is controversial &amp;mdash ; autism . But no , the science does not make it possible to take cord blood and , say , grow a new kidney , said Heidi Elmoazzen , the stem cells director at Canadian Blood Services who has a PhD in cryobiology. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;27523;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " alt= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;27559;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448089 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canadian Blood Services cord blood bank in Nepean is one of three such public banks in Canada ( Quebec has its own ) and preserves about 72 per cent of the agency&amp;rsquo ; s cord blood inventory , with the rest stored in Edmonton . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On any typical day , one to three donations will arrive at the bank&amp;rsquo ; s lab from the birthing unit at the General campus of The Ottawa Hospital , one of four hospitals in Canada where mothers of newborns may opt to donate the cord blood harvested from their newborn&amp;rsquo ; s umbilical cord . Mothers-to-be have to register before the birth to donate and agree again after the birth . The process doesn&amp;rsquo ; t hurt the mother or the baby &amp;mdash ; the umbilical cord is typically treated as medical waste , anyway . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Donors do it for altruistic reasons , to potentially help someone they will never meet . Still , &amp;ldquo ; it&amp;rsquo ; s quite an easy sell , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmoazzen. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are three ways to donate stem cells : through the blood , usually after the donor is given a drug that makes the stem cells exit bone arrow and enter the bloodstream , from the bone marrow itself , typically from the pelvic bone , and through cord blood . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As transplants go , stem cell transplants are relatively simple . The bag of frozen stem cells , which is stored in a box about the size of an audio cassette tape , is retrieved from the cryopreservation freezer by a robotic arm . Still frozen , tit is transported wherever it is needed in the world inside in a container that looks like a high-tech milk can . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When it gets to its destination , the unit is thawed . The patient , whose own blood production has been knocked out with chemotherapy , is transfused with the stem cells . If all goes well , within a few weeks the stem cells are repopulating the patient&amp;rsquo ; s body with healthy blood cells . The more closely the donor and the recipient are matched , the less likely the recipient will suffer graft vs. host disease , an immune condition that occurs when the donor&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;span class= " ILfuVd " &gt;&lt;span class= " e24Kjd " &gt;immune cells attack the recipient 's tissues . **26;27589;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Only about 14 per cent of the total 23,000 donations made in Canada since 2013 have been listed for possible matching . In the lab in Nepean , cord blood is tested for it suitability for donation . There are many reasons why a donation isn&amp;rsquo ; t eligible for transplant . The volume collected or the total nucleated cell count might be too low . The mother might have a health or social history that makes the donation ineligible . Or the cord blood might test positive for a transmissible disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The cord blood that does not qualify for donation can , with the mother&amp;rsquo ; s agreement , be used for research in cell therapy and transplant medicine . As of this year , the bank supports 17 cord-blood research projects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are a lot of moving parts to a complicated international system . Canadian Blood Services made a business case for opening its own cord blood banks . It costs the Canadian health system nothing for a cord blood unit from Canadian Blood Services . It costs about $40,000 U.S. for a unit from outside the country , said Todd Campbell , Canadian Blood Services&amp;rsquo ; business support specialist . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The international exchange of stem cells is a two-way street . About 60 per cent of Canadian donations have gone to recipients in other countries , but 80 per cent of Canadian patients receive stem cells from donors in other countries . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the average month , the bank will get 10 to 15 inquiries from transplant physicians around the world about a donation in one of the cord blood freezers . The units are listed in both a Canadian registry and an international database . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cord blood is often used to treat pediatric patients . One of its advantages is that can be retrieved and delivered very quickly . There are about 440,000 people on Canada&amp;rsquo ; s bone marrow registry , for example , but only about half of those who are approached actually agree to donate if they are requested . The reasons can vary &amp;mdash ; it might have been months or years since a potential donor signed up . The donor might be hard to locate , might have lost interest or have health problems . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada opened its first public cord-blood bank in 2013 . The goal was to create a multi-ethnic cord blood inventory to reflect the diversity of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s population . Since then , Canadian Blood Services has collected blood at four hospitals &amp;mdash ; in Ottawa , Edmonton , Brampton and Vancouver &amp;mdash ; and stores it in two banks , one in Ottawa and the other in Edmonton . The target was to get more than 60 per cent non-Caucasian donors . The bank has already exceeded that target . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re trying to build an inventory of cord blood to be able to transplant more patients in Canada , &amp;rdquo ; said Campbell . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;27617;TOOLONG ... title= " Medical laboratory technician Milenko Drajic checks for the growth of stem cells in a sample at the Nepean lab. " alt= " Medical laboratory technician Milenko Drajic checks for the growth of stem cells in a sample at the Nepean lab. " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;27653;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448088 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are also seven private cord blood banks in Canada where parents can opt to store their newborn&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood . However , there&amp;rsquo ; s a low probability of using one&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood for transplantation &amp;mdash ; between one in 20,000 and one in 250,000 , according to Health Canada . When a patient needs cord blood transplantation , cells from a healthy donor are preferable if privately banked blood cells carry the same genetic or congenital disorder that caused the disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A lot of people see ( private cord blood banking ) as an insurance policy . But if your child had leukemia , a physician would not use the child&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood . The genetic mutation is in the stem cells themselves , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmoazzen. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The other problem is that a patient sometimes needs more stem cells to be transplanted than those contained in a single cord blood unit . In most cases , even if parents had stored a unit for family use , it would likely not be sufficient for a successful transplantation , and additional units stored in public use banks would still be needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s like the dosage of medication . You need a minimum number of stem cells per kilogram of body weight , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmomazzen. &amp;ldquo ; A 20-pound patient needs less than an adult . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has a target of creating a bank of about 10,000 cord blood units . But that&amp;rsquo ; s a moving target which is re-evaluated regularly and the science evolves . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So far , 22 cord blood units have been withdrawn the Canadian public bank so far . Why so few ? Transplant surgeons have been looking to source stem cell donations not only from cord blood , but also from adult registries and family members of the patient . Even if a family member is a less-than-perfect match , graft vs. host disease can be managed using pharmaceuticals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the worldwide cord blood supply is growing quickly . There are 780,000 donated units available through the World Marrow Donor Association . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One of the system&amp;rsquo ; s biggest problems for the system is lack of awareness , said Elmoazzen . But that is changing . When the cord blood bank opened six years ago , about 32 per cent of new mothers consented to donate . That has since increased to 47 per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In an ideal world , it would like it to be like recycling . Everybody just knows about it and does it , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Cord blood by the numbers : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Minus 196 C : &lt;/strong&gt; Temperature at which cord blood is stored in liquid nitrogen &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;23,000 : &lt;/strong&gt; Qualified cord blood units collected since Canada&amp;rsquo ; s public bank launched in 2013 &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;3,300 : &lt;/strong&gt; Cord blood units stored and available for transplant &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;One in four : &lt;/strong&gt; Chance a patient needing a transplant will find a bone marrow donor match in his or her own family &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;$0 : &lt;/strong&gt; Costs to the Canadian medical system when a patient gets a cord blood donation from the Canadian Blood Services&amp;rsquo ; bank &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;$40,000 U.S : &lt;/strong&gt; Approximate cost if cord blood is sourced from elsewhere in the world &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;22 : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Withdrawals&amp;rdquo ; from the Canadian Blood Services cord blood bank since it was founded in 2013 &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27683;TOOLONG ... " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;27937;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1245893 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Children who are not getting enough sleep and spending a significant amount of time looking at screens have a higher likelihood of making poor decisions , a study published on Wednesday found . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Michelle Guerrero , lead author and postdoctoral fellow at the CHEO Research Institute and the University of Ottawa said her study looked at the correlation between screen time and behaviour in adolescents . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We were looking at how excessive screen time leads to impulsive behaviour , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Guerrero&amp;rsquo ; s study defined impulsive behaviour as acting &amp;ldquo ; without realizing the risk involved or the consequences involved with the behaviour . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Additionally , impulsive behaviour is often connected with mental health issues and is a key component of ADHD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When we don&amp;rsquo ; t think before we act&amp;hellip ; it has huge impacts on our lives , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Guerrero said a key discovery in the study was how easily preventable this behaviour is as it involves a minor life adjustment including less screen time and more sleep . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The behaviours we looked at in our study are modifiable , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &amp;ldquo ; They can be changed right now , today . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said her study found children who have their screen time limited to under two hours a day and sleep between nine to eleven hours a night &amp;ldquo ; are less impulsive . &amp;rdquo ; Exercise was also found to be a factor that led to less impulsive children . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There has been a significant amount of research on how screens can affect children&amp;rsquo ; s mental health , Guerrero said , and found the connection to impulsive behaviour unsurprising . Additionally , she said the benefit of a full-night&amp;rsquo ; s sleep is a major determinant of one&amp;rsquo ; s behaviour . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When people don&amp;rsquo ; t sleep long enough&amp;hellip ; Their behaviour is more impulsive , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The paper analysed data for 4,524 children and was titled 24-Hour Movement Behaviours and Impulsivity . It is part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study , which intends to follow participants for 10 years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The paper was published in Pediatrics and was authored by Guerrero alongside members of the Healthy Active Living and Obesity Research Group at the CHEO Research Institute . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27967;TOOLONG ... An additional 1,500 patients , who are not part of Health Links but also have high needs or difficulty getting to health appointments , also receive regular visits from Renfrew County community paramedics. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Community paramedics have become a key link in the chain that is the health system in Renfrew . They are helping to keep people out of hospital , reduce 911 calls and improve clients&amp;rsquo ; quality of life &amp;mdash ; and their families . Their work supports family physicians , community nurses and other health professionals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You become a family , &amp;rdquo ; says Rosemary Drziak . Nearby , three paramedic executives from Germany watched the demonstration closely . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Drones , which have delivered medicine to flood victims and given rescuers a birds-eye view of stranded homeowners in recent months , are just part of what drew the Germans to Renfrew County to see local paramedics at work . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They recently spent a week training with paramedics and taking notes . In addition to learning about the extensive use of drones , the Germans followed community paramedics doing their rounds visiting chronically ill patients in their homes . They also learned about technological innovations such as a specially designed electronic health records system for community para-medicine. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Germans are not the first to make the trek to the Ottawa Valley to learn from local paramedics . Renfrew County paramedics have helped rewrite the book on what it means to be a paramedic in a largely rural community . They have addressed challenges and changed local health care in the process . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The world is paying attention . But is the Ontario government ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;28712;TOOLONG ... title= " Brian Leahey ( centre ) , Deputy Chief of the Renfrew Paramedic Service , teaches Paramedic Sebastian Gerosch ( left ) and Paramedic Sebastian Lange about their drone program in Renfrew Thursday July 4 , 2019 . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;28748;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1432712 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Renfrew paramedic officials and politicians are concerned that changes announced by Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s Progressive Conservative government earlier this year could mean the loss of what makes the local paramedic service special . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Not only are its programs designed to meet specific needs of Renfrew residents and tackle difficult health and geographical challenges , but they are considered among the most innovative in the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Renfrew County , about an **25;28778;TOOLONG ; s drive northwest of Ottawa , the paramedic service functions as a kind of wire that connects and energizes all the components of the local health system . Their work in the community reduces hospital visits and stays by some of the highest-needs residents ; supports family medicine teams to help them function with large numbers of patients , as is common in rural areas ; and has technology to help remote residents remain in their homes and to deal with emergency situations . All that , in addition to the more traditional roles of responding to 911 calls , stabilizing sick patients and getting them to hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still , the future for Renfrew paramedics , and paramedics around the province , is unclear . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;28805;TOOLONG ... title= " Stephanie Rose , a community care paramedic , looks after Maria Makkos , 82 , during their initial consultation at Maria 's home in Arnrprior , July 10 , 2019. " alt= " Stephanie Rose , a community care paramedic , looks after Maria Makkos , 82 , during their initial consultation at Maria 's home in Arnrprior , July 10 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;28841;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1432715 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ontario government has announced it will amalgamate the 52 municipally run paramedic services across Ontario to create 10 regional services . Along with amalgamation will come upgraded communications systems , says Health Minister Christine Elliott , who promises it will result in a more efficient and effective system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt; " By better integrating dispatch and paramedic services , the ministry will improve coordination and ensure that resources are being used for frontline patient care in a model that is sustainable for the years to come , " said health ministry spokesman Mark Nesbitt in a statement . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Renfrew paramedic officials say they want to make sure the government knows the kind of work being done across the county and in other parts of the province before it makes massive changes . &lt;/p&gt; **28;28871;TOOLONG : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;28901;TOOLONG ... know they are not alone ' : In Renfrew , community paramedics make house calls and change **26;28936;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; Chief Mike Nolan argues that the Renfrew paramedic services is achieving exactly what the province wants with its reset of the health system . Renfrew&amp;rsquo ; s innovative community paramedic program has reduced 911 calls by 24 per cent among a population of chronically ill residents who have been frequent 911 users in the past . The result is improved individual health outcomes at a lower cost to the health system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The program that we are running in Renfrew County fulfills and , in many cases , exceeds the interests of this government in reforming the health-care system , &amp;rdquo ; says Nolan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nolan says Renfrew County officials want to inform the province that there are models of care in place &amp;mdash ; in Renfrew and elsewhere &amp;mdash ; that should be expanded across the province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His concern is that amalgamation will water down paramedic programs to &amp;ldquo ; the lowest common denominator&amp;rdquo ; which will mean the loss of innovation , technological advances and local relevance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nolan and others are hoping to lead changes to paramedic services across the country and see those innovations expanded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;28964;TOOLONG ... title= " Renfrew paramedic chief Mike Nolan . " alt= " Renfrew paramedic chief Mike Nolan . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;29000;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1432714 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Renfrew paramedics have already helped drive change in paramedic services across Ontario and around the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When it comes to community paramedics , Renfrew County is known as one of the leading programs in the world , says Sebastian Lange , one of the visiting Bavarian paramedics . Renfrew has also seen experts fly in from Ireland , England , Australia , New Zealand , the U.S. , Turkey , the Netherlands and several other Canadian provinces to learn about its paramedic model . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The county is the largest , geographically , in the province &amp;mdash ; stretching from Ottawa to Algonquin Park &amp;mdash ; and , like many rural parts of the province , serves a population that is older , has lower socioeconomic status and is more likely to have chronic disease than more urban parts of the province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Its use of technology is , in part , an answer to some of those geographic challenges . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Renfrew County paramedic services pioneered the use of drone technology to assist first responders . It has worked closely with Transport Canada and is the only paramedic organization in the country that has permission to use drones beyond the line of sight , says deputy chief Brian Leahey , who is in charge of the program . Leahey is also a pilot . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Drones are used frequently by Renfrew paramedics , for a variety of tasks . They can deliver supplies , and defibrillators , to remote areas faster than paramedics can get there . In fact , paramedics are looking at keeping a permanent drone on location to deliver defibrillators to more isolated parts of the county . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Recently , drones have also been used to assess emergency situations &amp;mdash ; including in flood zones or accident scenes . The unmanned aerial system , as it is known , works closely with the service&amp;rsquo ; s remote access team , and others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The community paramedic program tackles demographic challenges in Renfrew County by making house calls and doing remote monitoring of some of the sickest patients in the area . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Bill Craig is among its clients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Craig , 64 , of Arnprior , is a diabetic and kidney transplant patient who was a frequent user of 911 services until the community medicine program began monitoring him 24/7. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Community paramedics would visit him at home regularly to check his blood pressure and blood sugar , among other things . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I have found it really beneficial , &amp;rdquo ; says Craig . &amp;ldquo ; When they leave here , they don&amp;rsquo ; t just leave , they follow-up with your family doctor and they research different things . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Paramedics have even travelled with Craig to visit his endocrinologist in Ottawa to better understand his medical needs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Craig says he feels more secure under the watchful eye of the community paramedic program . Paramedics have discovered him , more than once , in a diabetic coma when they came for a visit . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The service works with family health teams and other medical professionals , remotely monitors some patients and is available 24/7. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Community paramedics monitor some high-needs patients with electronic systems that send digital information back to the paramedics , such as blood pressure and weight . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;29030;TOOLONG ... title= " Stephanie Rose , a community care paramedic , chats with Bill Craig , a patient at his home in Arnrprior , July 10 , 2019. " alt= " Stephanie Rose , a community care paramedic , chats with Bill Craig , a patient at his home in Arnrprior , July 10 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;29066;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1432717 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Paramedics are alerted when readings are abnormal or when readings have been missed , which can trigger a visit to the patient at home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Community paramedics also operate mobile clinics around the county that offer medical services where seniors are . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s kind of like a barber shop , in that we go to where the seniors are playing euchre and set up the corner , &amp;rdquo ; says Nolan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; People bring their medications and are given help keeping track of them . The paramedics take blood pressure , offer electro cardio grams and blood tests . &amp;ldquo ; It is not uncommon that we pick up patients that have high blood pressure . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A group of 20 community paramedics see more than 1,500 clients regularly . They monitor up to 150 patients in their homes &amp;mdash ; most of them among the five per cent of patients who use 80 per cent of health services , including Craig . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They tend to be socio-economically challenged , which is an indicator of the challenges they face managing their health , &amp;rdquo ; says Nolan . &amp;ldquo ; For many of these people , to take a taxi to go to the lab to get blood work done and to go home is a choice of whether they are going to eat that day or not , or turn up the thermostat . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Community paramedics keep in close touch with their clients&amp;rsquo ; family physicians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;29096;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jeff Dodge , a former Ottawa high-tech CEO who became a Renfrew paramedic as a second career , has been key to developing some of the Renfrew paramedic organization&amp;rsquo ; s high-tech expertise . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Working with the Quebec-based software company Prehos , the paramedic service developed an electronic records system for community paramedics . It went live in Renfrew County last year and is now used by the majority of paramedic services in Eastern Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Using the system , community paramedics have access to client records on tablets and can share notes and data with family doctors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dodge , who makes home visits as a community paramedic , recalls writing a note to a client&amp;rsquo ; s doctor after one of his visits . &amp;ldquo ; Before I left the house , the doctor had it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;29132;TOOLONG ... title= " Stephanie Rose , a community care paramedic , looks after Ed Pinnell at his home in Arnrprior July 10 , 2019.
